title: Apple blocks web certificates that could be used by scammers, but Mac vulnerability remains
snippet: Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites. However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … more…
fullText:
Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites.

However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … 

The issue concerns what are known as intermediate certificates. These are used to prove ownership of a website, so if you visit apple.com, for example, Safari will check that you are visiting the real site.

However, an error in a script used to generate these certificates led to a number of private keys that could be trivially discovered by testing just 256 possible numbers. The eight compromised certificates have now been revoked, and steps taken to ensure that the vulnerability won’t affect any future certificates issued.

Bleeping Computer reports that Apple, Google and Mozilla have each blocked the compromised certificates in their respective web browsers. However, Mozilla cryptography engineer Dennis Jackson warns that Macs may continue to trust them.

Jackson also warns that macOS’s built-in /usr/bin/curl utility may continue trusting the compromised certificates because its certificate bundle does not check revocation information.

In other words, if your Mac has already accepted one of the certificates, then it will continue to do so. However, there is currently no evidence of them being used in the wild, and it’s something that Apple is likely to be able to fix in an upcoming security update.

fullText:
The popular retro game emulator Delta has today launched a big new 2.0 version, most notably featuring a refreshed Liquid Glass interface and support for the iPhone Duo.

The app now has specially-designed controller skins that are optimized for all the different iPhone Duo poses, including some beautiful Nintendo DS layouts that use the full size of the inner display, and cleverly spans the crease when partially folded in book mode in portrait. 

The bigger screen of the iPhone Duo enables some immersive gaming experiences, but the Delta developers have also ensured that the app naturally reflows on the portrait closed outer screen too. 

Another little easter egg is that you can fold the Duo closed to automatically put the DS to sleep, emulating the physical behavior of a real DS console.

Delta also has a special trick when using it in landscape split view alongside another app. You can see it in action in this screenshot, which depicts Delta running side by side with another iPhone Duo app that is playing a video. 

Typically, the iPhone Duo Split View means each app is constrained to 50% of the screen space. But, as shown in this example, because the app exposes the bottom half of the virtual DS as a custom keyboard view, the system allows this ‘keyboard’ to stretch across the full width of the screen, overlapping the unrelated video player app on the other side of the split. 

Aside from iPhone Duo support, the new update also includes Sega Genesis ROM compatibility, improved library navigation, updated audio settings that allow game audio to mix alongside your currently playing music or podcast, and more. 

The premium version of Delta can be unlocked using an In-App Purchase subscription directly through the App Store, now available worldwide. In the US, EU, Brazil, and Japan, you can also support the app directly through Patreon.

title: As iPhone Duo Cracked Screen Reports Surface, a New Teardown Shows a Possible Culprit
snippet: In spite of its display issues, iFixit declares the iPhone Duo “the most repairable foldable” it’s ever tinkered with.
fullText:
With official reviews out in the world, you might assume there’s little left to say about the iPhone Duo that hasn’t already been said. But this is a long-awaited Apple product we’re talking about, and ongoing scrutiny of this show-stealer of a device is not just desirable, it’s pretty much mandatory.

This is because, while we’ve loved using the device so far and think Apple’s first attempt at a foldable is admirable, some early iPhone Duo owners have reported problems with the screen. 

We’re currently conducting our own testing on the screen, folding the iPhone Duo 900 times per hour with a custom-made machine to see how long its hinge will last. At the time of writing, it had passed 20,000 folds without issue, but other people with a Duo haven’t been so lucky. Most commonly, people have reported issues with display cracks and lines of faulty pixels appearing along the hinge, according to MacRumors and Reddit.

			

More from CNET

As quickly as the faults have come to light, repairability experts at iFixit think they might already have discovered the culprit. Using teardown footage, patents and CT scans it collected while breaking down the iPhone Duo to ascertain its repairability score, iFixit built a 3D hinge model to identify where things could be going wrong.

What it found was that the breaks seemed to be occurring in the same place: just below the cable that connects the two screens, in a spot where a bunch of different connectors all meet. 

“All those edges meeting in this spot mean lots of possible culprits,” said iFixit in a blog post. “That center pivot looks different from the rest of the hinge. Could it be getting stuck? Could something else be getting stuck?

“Here’s one possible answer. In our closing simulation… the center support bar fails to drop far enough. The screen’s curved fold comes down onto it, creating a small stress hotspot near the reported break location.”

iFixit has created an interactive CT scan that allows you to play around with the Duo and see how the hinge supports, cable, and nearby components fit beneath the display.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to request for comment about the faults, but anyone experiencing issues with their iPhone Duo should be protected under warranty at this stage. Apple will charge $999 for inner screen replacement at a later date — whether that makes an AppleCare subscription a worthwhile investment is a choice only you can make.

The “most repairable foldable”

Any reports of screen problems are obviously bad news for Apple, but the company does also have reason to be proud of itself. 

iFixit has declared the iPhone Duo “the most repairable foldable smartphone we’ve ever taken apart.” The phone has scored a 5/10 repairability rating, which might not be as impressive as the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max’s scores of 7/10, but still makes Apple the industry leader in terms of foldable repairaibility.

In its teardown, iFixit called out the trim surrounding the Duo’s screen as being particularly easy to pull away in contrast to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8’s trim, which “crumbled” as it was removed. The flat layout of the Duo’s components also garnered praise from iFixit. Being able to access things like the cameras and logic board without having to take the whole device apart makes for a simpler repair if one of those individual components requires replacement.

iFixit praised the flat layout of the Duo’s internal components.iFixit/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

iFixit also praised Apple’s electrically releasable adhesive, which can be used to easily remove the battery by passing a low voltage through it. This is an innovative repair technology that Apple pioneered and is also used across its other devices. It allows the cells to be removed without any bending or prying that could result in a puncture risk to the battery.

Finally, a key part of making tech more repairable is ensuring that the companies making the products also make instruction manuals and official parts accessible to people — whether they’re doing the repairs themselves at home, or taking them to a third-party repair shop. iFixit is still awaiting official parts from Apple, but it praised the company for publishing its repair manual so quickly.

Major points were deducted for the hinge and inner display — both of which would be difficult and time consuming to repair.

“For a first attempt, Apple has done well,” said iFixit. “The easy battery removal alone is something we’d like to see on every foldable. But of course we’ll hold Apple accountable for making replacement parts available, and here’s hoping that the next generation of the Duo features a more affordable inner display and a more accessible hinge repair.”

YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar.

On mobile, YouTube is “kicking off a series of updates to shape a more seamless Home experience.” This starts with a redesigned top bar with dedicated feeds.

As part of this change, YouTube is removing the Subscriptions tab from its fourth position in the bottom bar. It’s now in the “top bar on the Home tab.” Testing of the redesign started earlier this year. 

“Subs” appears in the second position after “Home” with a red underline that will take some getting used to. This change will break a lot of muscle memory, with Subscriptions appearing in the YouTube bottom bar for nearly a decade (2017).

	

Old vs. new

Meanwhile, after Subs, you’ll see new dedicated feeds for Live, Music, and Movies & TV, with the latter only appearing if you have active subscriptions (such as Primetime Channels). This change has the upside of removing YouTube’s navigation drawer. 

	

More broadly, this change coincides with the launch of custom feeds, which are also available on and sync to the web. This lets you describe “what you want to see in your own words”.

Tap “+” at the top of your Home feed and describe the topic, channels, or vibe you’re looking for (for example, “help me unwind after work with guided meditations under 10 minutes”). You’ll then get a new feed tailored to your interests for you to explore.

They will appear as top tabs in the main feed after Home and Subs so that “you can jump back into them whenever you want.” The prompt box at the top of each feed lets you change it.

Notably, free users “can save up to 3 active custom feeds, while YouTube Premium members can save up to 8.”

Custom feeds are first rolling out on “mobile and desktop in English to U.S. based, signed-in viewers.” It will be available in more countries going forward.

title: Some Galaxy S24, S25 owners say Samsung’s latest update is wrecking battery life
snippet: Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.” more…
fullText:
Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.”

It’s an age-old story. Major update on a last-gen device and battery life, at least for some users, gets worse. It’s something you hate to see, but it’s a pretty established pattern at this point. 

Reports have popped up since the update started rolling out more widely. SammyFans spotted a report of one user whose phone died in just over 5 hours, admittedly on heavy use. Meanwhile, there are also reports on Galaxy S25 series devices, including one user who now has to “charge my phone 3 to 4 times a day,” with others mirroring that problem. 

This seems to be the oddity and not the norm, so far at least. These reports aren’t widespread, nor are droves of other users reporting the exact same problem. Some troubleshooting steps that can help range from a simple reboot, force-stopping rogue apps, or a factory reset. Major system updates like this, as mentioned, just tend to go a little rogue sometimes.

title: Someone built iPhone Duo’s tent mode for Android foldables, but made it even better
snippet: Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing. more…
fullText:
Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing.

One iPhone Duo feature that isn’t widely used on Android is the ability to show information while in “Tent Mode.” The Motorola Razr Fold is one of the few book-style foldables with this feature as a part of its always-on display, but the iPhone Duo’s “StandBy” mode is one that folks could easily want on other devices. Pixel also has similar functionality, but only while charging. 

A new Android app that delivers something pretty close to iPhone Duo’s tent mode is “Foldy.” 

The app is free to use, but requires a premium unlock (90¢/month or $9 lifetime) for its most useful features. On my Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app quickly let me turn tent mode into a useful dual-pane hub that shows the date and time, or data from my calendar. 

	

Its most useful functionality, though, is the ability to turn any Android widget into a pane, opening the door to useful functions such as Google Home or music app controls.

“Foldy” also lets you “train” the app to know when to activate. This works very well, with the app recognizing when the device is partially open and on its side, activating the “StandBy” clone as soon as the conditions are right.

Another example of Android developers quickly coming up with their own takes on iPhone Duo apps is “Foldman,” an app that turns your foldable into a Walkman-style casette player. It’s similar to a Duo app that’s been widely talked about, but with some added bonuses such as YouTube Music integration.

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music

Is this a bad thing? No! One of the biggest benefits that Apple’s entrance to the foldable space was going to bring was helping to build out new app experiences for Android foldables. I can’t wait for this sort of effort to expand to many more Android apps and experiences.

title: iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is it a Galaxy Fold moment?
snippet: Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both? more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both?

The earliest days of Android foldables were turbulent, to say the least. The original Galaxy Fold ran into major display issues within just 48 hours of reviewers getting their hands on the phone prior to the official release, leading to Samsung ultimately delaying the Galaxy Fold’s release for months. Part of the issue at the time was that curious minds were removing the top-layer screen protector that, as every foldable now makes abundantly clear, was never meant to be removed. The other problem came in the form of debris that would get under the display and kill the panel from underneath.

During the delay, Samsung ended up making some updates to the Galaxy Fold’s design, including making the top layer extend under the bezel, adding caps to the top and bottom of the hinge to prevent dust and debris from getting under the display panel, and reinforcing the display itself to protect it. At the time, Samsung’s CEO admitted that the launch was “pushed… before it was ready,” leading to the “embarassing” delay.

Galaxy Fold display failures from 2019 from The Verge

Now, Apple seems to be running into its own first-gen foldable issues.

	

As our sister site 9to5Mac highlights, there are a growing number of reports of early iPhone Duo units breaking, with the inner display failing in the exact same way across a number of units. The display fails in the middle, with a green line forming across the right side of the panel before further damage develops over time. 

The cause of the failure, it seems is a flaw in Apple’s hinge design. iFixit hypoethsizes that a support bar isn’t dropping far enough to leave room for the display panel, in turn creating a point of stress that could explain the broken iPhone Duo displays.

Similarly, iFixit’s teardown of the original Galaxy Fold in 2019 seemed to reveal the cause of Samsung’s display failures – and ended up being very much on the right track based on Samsung’s later fixes – though iFixit ended up removing the teardown at Samsung’s request. 

Another YouTuber has found a similar point of failure in the iPhone Duo’s hinge that seems to point to why displays are breaking the in same location. Affected users have found that the hinge has resistance before the display cracks, including an “audible crack.” 

In Samsung’s case, the problem was two-fold (pun intended), with some clear flaws in the hinge design and user error in the removal of the top layer. Samsung responded by delaying the release and making adjustments before re-releasing its first-gen foldable.

In Apple’s case, it’s certainly a bit trickier as this problem wasn’t revealed until the iPhone Duo landed in the hands of customers. The company has yet to issue a formal response to the problem, and affected users seem to be getting mixed messages from support channels. It’s still unclear in the chaos of the iPhone Duo’s launch just how widespread the issue is.

What do you think of the iPhone Duo’s display failures? Coincdence, or a bigger problem?

title: Some seven years later, the iTunes Store is making an unlikely come-back
snippet: Please accept my apologies if the headline made you feel old, but yes, Apple retired the iTunes desktop app way back in 2019. However, a new report says that the iTunes Store is currently experiencing an unlikely seeming revival. This is thanks to a tactic being used by artists like Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and more … more…
fullText:
Please accept my apologies if the headline made you feel old, but yes, Apple retired the iTunes desktop app way back in 2019. However, a new report says that the iTunes Store is currently experiencing an unlikely seeming revival.

This is thanks to a tactic being used by artists like Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and more … 

The iTunes Store revolutionized the way people bought music, not only prompting digital sales over physical, but allowing people to buy individual songs rather than an entire album. By the summer of 2019, however, Apple retired the iTunes Mac app in favor of new music, podcasts, and TV apps. 

The world has largely switched to streaming services, with relatively few people buying music outright, but the Financial Times reports that there is a countermovement underway.

The iTunes Store is re-emerging as an unlikely venue for pop stars to hawk collectibles to superfans, reach untapped audiences, and bolster chart positions. Last month, pop superstar Ariana Grande surprise-released a live version of her latest album Petal as an iTunes-only exclusive. This follows a string of iTunes-exclusive releases in recent years from artists such as Taylor Swift, Charli XCX, Doja Cat, Summer Walker and Tinashe.

Swift is perhaps the best example. The FT reports that her Life of a Showgirl album did better from physical and digital sales in its first week in the US than it did on streaming services. When Ariana Grande announced a surprise release of a live version of her Petal album on iTunes, it jumped from number 15 to number 6 in the charts. Charli XCX went further by making the B-side songs to her Music, Fashion, Film album an iTunes exclusive.

A report back in February said that Apple was still marketing iTunes to music labels.

Industry experts have mixed views on how well the strategy is likely to work more broadly, but it’s certainly an interesting trend.

title: YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening
snippet: Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is. more…
fullText:
Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is.

The dislike button has been a topic of contention in the YouTube community for years now, ever since YouTube removed the count that showed alongside it. So when some users noticed that the dislike button was suddenly no longer visible and hidden behind an overflow menu, there was plenty of confusion around the change.

In a statement to 9to5Google, though, YouTube directly confirms that this is not a test or a change that you’ll see on YouTube videos. Rather, this update to the dislike button’s location appears solely on the video page for a creator’s own video. In other words, you’ll only see this altered location on your own videos.

A YouTube spokesperson explains:

	

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

And, sure enough, we were able to immediately replicate this behavior when we tested it out on one of our own videos.

title: I needed a dashcam while out running. Meta glasses turned out to be the answer
snippet: I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair. more…
fullText:
I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair.

This summer, I did something I never thought I would do: I started running. “But Nick, why are you running if nothing is chasing you?” my friends joked snarkily. The reality is, yes, I do often run a little faster at times to avoid getting hit by a car, something that’s particularly problematic any time I have to cross a road (even if there’s a crosswalk).

That got me thinking. If cars have dashcams, what could someone do to help document a potential accident? There’s no chance I’m running while holding my phone, and I wouldn’t want it in my pocket either. I also wouldn’t be able to pull it out of one of those armband holsters fast enough to video a potential accident, either. Then I realized the answer was already on my face: my Meta glasses.

I’d already been taking my glasses out on every run to make short video clips to post to my Strava account — with my smartwatch health stats plastered on the video, too — so it made a lot of sense to just take a few more clips along the way. Now I have a personal running dashcam at all times, and it takes less than a second to capture a video whenever I need it.

	

Is this really convenient?

Maybe surprisingly, yes, using Meta glasses as a dashcam is quite convenient. Since I already wore my Meta Nova and Oakley Meta HSTN glasses on regular runs, I didn’t have to significantly change my behavior. I already look out for cars when I cross the street (my mama taught me well); all I have to do now is hold the camera button to start a video recording if I see one coming.

I’ve got my Meta glasses set to record 3 minutes at a time, so I’m not worried about missing a potential problem because the recording got cut short. Once I cross the road, I just press the button again and manually stop the recording.

	

Everything is saved to the glasses until it reconnects to my phone; then everything is synced automatically at that time. It’s as effortless as you can get, and it’s impressively good insurance if anything were to go awry on a run.

If I had to buy a new pair of Meta glasses today, there’s little chance I’d buy one without a camera. While there’s been some negativity surrounding the inclusion of the camera, there are far too many good reasons to have it available to use.

Runners who want to try this should give the Oakley Meta HSTN glasses a shot first, as they’ve got the tightest fit and the most “runner-like” style. Otherwise, the cheaper Meta-branded glasses (read: no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding onboard) are a better budget choice, especially since there’s no functional difference between any of Meta’s latest pairs. And, if you really want to stay away from Meta, Rokid AI Glasses are the best alternative I’ve used to date.

fullText:
Get month-long battery life, physical watch hands, all the health tracking you need, and more for just $249 with this Garmin Instinct Crossover deal.

When you can’t decide between a “regular” watch and a smartwatch, a hybrid is the way to go. Just as it sounds, the Garmin Instinct Crossover successfully marries the physical, tactile feel of a standard sports watch with the usefulness and health-tracking wizardry of a smartwatch. It’s even got dope glow-in-the-dark hands and numbers, plus a bright backlit display, making it easy to see in any light (or none at all).

This Garmin Instinct Crossover deal takes $50 off the regular price (that’s just $5 away from the lowest price of all time). This one’s a 2022 release, and while that would be old for a Wear OS watch, Garmin is good about supporting their watches for a very long time. The company does sell a newer version of this watch with an AMOLED display, but it’s a whopping $649, and I’m not sure it’s worth $400 more.

Despite having physical hands, the Instinct Crossover sports all the amazing, uh, sports-tracking features of the Instinct 2 series. It’s seriously cool to watch it in action!

	

Garmin Instinct Crossover at Amazon

And yes, that means you can connect it with Meta AI Glasses and see your real-time workout stats on any videos you record during your runs, workouts, or whatever it is you like to do. And, yes, you can still see all your notifications on the watch face.

At $400 cheaper than the newest model and $50 less than the usual price, this Garmin Instinct Crossover deal is one to seriously consider.

title: Apple must open iPhone to alternative app stores in Australia after Epic Games ruling
snippet: An Australian federal judge has ordered Apple to make sweeping changes to its App Store rules following a years-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. Apple has confirmed that it plans to appeal. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
An Australian federal judge has ordered Apple to make sweeping changes to its App Store rules following a years-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. Apple has confirmed that it plans to appeal. Here are the details.

Epic scores major victory in Australia

Apple must allow iPhone users with Australian Apple Accounts to install apps from third-party app stores and websites starting March 1, 2027, a federal judge ordered today in a 235-page decision. Apple has until February 15 to request an extension until May 3, 2027, subject to court approval.

Today’s order follows a ruling last year that Apple violated Australian competition law by restricting alternative app distribution and payment methods, in a lawsuit brought by Epic Games similar to its long-running legal battle with Apple in the US.

In his decision, Justice Jonathan Beach said Apple held “a substantial degree of power in the iOS app distribution services market and the iOS in-app payment solutions market,” and used its developer agreements and App Store guidelines to restrict competition.

Among the practices singled out by the judge were:

Blocking app downloads and installations outside the App Store

Preventing developers from distributing apps through alternative channels

Requiring developers to use Apple’s in-app payment system

Prohibiting links to alternative payment methods

Requiring developers to offer content purchased elsewhere through Apple’s in-app purchase system as well.

Preventing developers from handling refunds directly

The ruling also cited Apple’s actions against Epic Games in 2020, including its refusal to allow Epic Direct Pay, Fortnite’s removal from the App Store, and the subsequent termination of Epic’s developer account.

Justice Beach described the latter two actions as “a paradigm example of Apple’s enforcement of its restrictive terms, in contravention of” section 46 of Australia’s Competition and Consumer Act 2010, which prohibits corporations with substantial market power from engaging in conduct that has “the purpose, or has or is likely to have the effect, of substantially lessening competition” in that market.

As a result, Justice Beach issued a wide-ranging series of orders requiring Apple to, among other things:

Allow alternative app stores and sideloading: Let Australian iPhone users download and install apps directly from websites and third-party marketplaces.

Allow alternative payment methods: Let developers use payment systems other than Apple’s, including within apps distributed through the App Store.

Permit external payment links: Allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods from within their apps.

Provide access to developer tools: Make the APIs and tools necessary for alternative app distribution available on substantially the same terms as those offered to App Store developers.

Restrict fees and other barriers: Prohibit fees for accessing alternative distribution channels, limit certain fees on external payments, and allow developers to offer lower prices outside Apple’s payment system.

Readmit Epic Games’ apps: Allow Fortnite and other eligible Epic Games apps back onto the Australian App Store, subject to compliance with applicable developer rules. (Importantly, this specific order is not subject to the March 2027 deadline, but rather takes effect immediately, with Apple required to act upon receiving a written application from Epic.)

The decision also addresses several other aspects of Apple’s App Store policies, including restrictions on its ability to turn off apps installed outside the App Store and requirements related to notarization.

The court also prohibited Apple from requiring developers to report transactions processed through alternative payment providers or offer Apple’s payment system alongside their preferred alternatives, both of which are requirements the company imposes in other regions, including Brazil and Japan.

When it comes to Apple’s wins in the decision, the list is much slimmer. Judge Beach rejected Epic’s request to extend the court’s injunctions worldwide and allowed Apple to maintain security scanning and notarization requirements for apps distributed outside the App Store. And while Apple must permit competing app marketplaces on iOS, it is not required to distribute them through its own App Store. This is a distinction he had already established in last year’s ruling.

Finally, the court ordered Apple to pay 85% of Epic’s legal costs incurred through the original trial, while reserving a decision on costs associated with the subsequent hearings over remedies.

	

Commenting on the decision, Epic confirmed “Fortnite is coming back to the App Store in Australia tomorrow,” and celebrated it as “great news for developers worldwide and iOS users in Australia who will benefit from an open mobile app ecosystem.”

In a statement to Reuters, Apple said:

“We will request a stay and appeal the outcome to seek a resolution ​that ​respects our ⁠intellectual property and protects the safe, ​secure experience that consumers ​and ⁠developers expect from the App Store.”

title: Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music
snippet: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon.

Foldables sort of walk that dichotomic line between nostalgic and futuristic. They remind us of flip phones from the 2000s, while running on an entirely different decade of tech.

Naturally, a Walkman-style app is a welcome addition to something like the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

One user developed an app called “Foldman” that uses your music from local storage or other apps and plays them in a virtual tape deck. On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app’s facade looks just like a cassette player. The app expands to show a wider stereo visual when the phone is opened up.

	

There’s a ton of cool little touches, like a volume slider and running tape counter on the virtual player. And the tape actually transfers from one tape reel to the other instead of a looping animation with no progressive movement! That’s such a nice little detail.

A Walkman-esque app fits so well on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 because of how wide and short the front display is, just like Sony’s original cassette player. That form factor is becoming increasingly popular, and it’s creating opportunities for some cool apps like this.

The app’s developer plans to integrate Spotify within the next couple of days and cautions that this early version has some rough edges. For now, it works with YouTube Music and Apple Music, as well as with files stored locally. The app is free and open source, stripped of ads or tracking.

We never recommend users download APKs outside of verified app stores, so do so at your own risk.

Beyond Spotify, they note that they’re looking into adding support for self-hosted streaming services, so users can use it with their existing library of digital files on their network. For now, it’s a simple little Walkman-style player, and that’s cool enough.

title: Here’s What Happens to Bacon When You Add Water While Cooking
snippet: Water and greasy bacon sound like a recipe for hot splatter. Here’s how the viral hack actually works.
fullText:
Charred and crisp, softer with a chewy middle: no matter how you cook your pork belly, bacon rules the roost among craveable breakfast meats. A handful of ways exist to make the salty strips, but a TikTok cooking hack that calls for a few ounces of water while cooking is making the rounds. The claim is that it even cooks the bacon, prevents dangerous oil splatters and keeps the meat from burning beyond recognition. 

But does it work?

Though I’m a fan of the quick, easy, CNET-approved oven-baking technique and even speedier air fryer method, the water-cooked method allegedly renders the bacon’s fat slowly and consistently, resulting in uniform cooking, fewer splatters and even reduced sodium. 

			

More from CNET

Not one to take social media’s word for it, I put the viral bacon hack to the test.

The water-cooked bacon trick

The technique couldn’t be simpler.Joey Skladany/CNET

The stovetop process is simple: 

Place bacon slices in an oversized skillet so they lie flat. 

Add ¼ cup of water to the skillet and cook over medium heat. 

Allow the water to steam and evaporate. Once the water is gone, lower the heat to medium-low and cook the bacon until it reaches your desired crispiness. 

Remove the cooked bacon from the skillet and place on a paper towel to soak up excess oil. 

I assumed the water would cause grease bombs, but it did the opposite. Joey Skladany/CNET

Ultimately, the water is said to suppress hot grease from popping violently and landing on stovetops or, more importantly, your skin. It also lets the meat cook low and slow before it fries in its own grease, rather than crisping immediately as the skillet heats up.  

Water can also draw out some of the bacon’s sodium, which is ideal for those who find it too salty. 

The results

The bacon turned out crisp with a slight chew.Joey Skladany/CNET

Color me shocked by the results: This cooking tip was executed flawlessly and lived up to the hype. The bacon strips were chewy yet crispy, with no bitter char, and cleanup took mere seconds with a quick wipe with a sponge and towel. (Pro tip: Reserve the leftover bacon grease to cook everything, from vegetables to rice, for added flavor.)

My only gripe was that it took a few minutes longer than using an oven or cast-iron skillet. And, frankly, the cleanup of pesky splatters would far surpass the time it takes to cook with water, at least with the latter tool. 

TikTok cooking tips are a mixed bag, but this bacon hack proved itself a winner.Joey Skladany/CNET

In an industry full of gimmicks and unverifiable shortcuts, it’s nice to sift through the culinary fluff and find something that actually works, especially with an ingredient as universally beloved as bacon. The fact that this trick has trended on TikTok is just a footnote and proof that social media sometimes gets it right. 

Hungry for more tips? Here’s how to recycle frying oil, plus a neat trick for degreasing a frying pan before washing.

title: iPhone Duo Owners: Your Apps Will Look Better Soon
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has new screen dimensions, leaving apps with a lot of unused space or awkward cropping. It’ll get better over time.
fullText:
For some lucky Apple superfans, today is the day they get to unbox their iPhone Duo. (Others may have to wait until January.) But after formally transferring all their software, they’ll discover a troubling truth: Some of their favorite apps look bad, with awkwardly unused space. 

Yet the message from CNET phone reviewers over the decades is reassuring. If precedent is anything to go by, updates will be coming to adjust apps to the iPhone Duo’s novel screen ratios, from the squat and wide front screen to the 4:3 inner display. Don’t worry — your apps will get better (and some are already tuned to the device’s dimensions).

That may be little comfort for Duo owners looking forlornly at Android foldables, which have had the better part of a decade on the market for app makers to adjust to the new formats. Despite having a similar passport-sized format to Apple’s foldable, most apps are sized correctly for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

But that wasn’t the case with the first Samsung Galaxy Fold, which launched in early 2019, as CNET Editor at Large Andy Lanxon recalls. 

“I had exactly the same experience when I used the first Samsung Galaxy Fold on the day it came out, with many apps appearing to be oddly squashed into that larger inner display,” Lanxon said. “Over time, both Android and foldable makers like Samsung and Google developed better software to accommodate foldables, and I’m confident that Apple won’t take long to patch up any shortcomings in this area.”

		

			

Indeed, it’s easy to forget that as the world’s first mainstream foldable, the original Galaxy Fold launched with plenty of display, hinge and other hardware problems that were ironed out over the years. Apple’s first foldable benefits from that refinement, launching with a minimal crease, a smooth and seemingly durable hinge, internal software suited to a folding screen (with FOMO-inspiring animations), IP68 dust- and water-resistance and other qualities that ease use.

The Duo also benefits from being a single design, as opposed to the various screen sizes and formats across all the Android foldables. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, for instance, both have 6.5-inch outer screens and 8-inch inner screens, but the former is slightly wider yet shorter than the latter. 

Read more: New iPhone Duo? Here are 4 Features You Should Check Out Now

The iPhone Duo’s inner and outer screens have the same ratio.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

But it’s the Duo’s specific design that might also accelerate app adjustment, Lanxon notes: The outer display has the same aspect ratio as the larger inner display, something Apple highlighted during its Sept. 9 presentation launching the device. So developers only need to design one app size for the Duo that will work perfectly well on both displays. 

Compare that to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which pairs a tall and narrow 21:9 cover screen with an almost square 10:9 inner screen.

That’s somewhat reassuring, but what iPhone Duo owners likely want to know is: When will my apps get updated? To predict that, we look to the past — both the development of other foldables and the radical changes in Apple’s own iPhone line.

The iPhone X, revealed on stage in October 2017, shifted to an all-glass front panel and the notorious notch at the top, requiring apps to adjust. 

Apple / Screenshot by Sarah Tew

Remembering when apps had to adapt to new screens

Given how long smartphones have had all-glass front panels, it’s understandable that it takes time to adapt apps to foldable displays. But it’s easy to forget that app makers had to go through the same process before when phones finally ditched physical buttons below screens for the all-glass front to begin with. 

“I remember when the iPhone X came out, and apps that hadn’t been optimized had black bars above and below,” said CNET Editor at Large Scott Stein, who reviewed the device back in 2017. “It meant all apps didn’t initially make the most of the new phone’s size.” 

The Duo will have the same growing pains until more apps get optimized, Stein added — it takes time, and it’s part of what it means to be a hardware early adopter. 

The original Samsung Galaxy Fold, launched in Feb. 2019.

Sarah Tew/CNET

It’s important to remember how complex it is to make software for a foldable, as explained by Jessica Dolcourt, CNET Group and CNET Labs vice president of content operations and commerce. When you open and close a foldable device, you’re asking your app to perform acrobatics, instantly leaping between internal and external displays while simultaneously expanding or contracting the view window and rearranging all the pixels. 

Dolcourt spent over a decade reviewing phones for CNET, including the original Samsung Galaxy Fold in 2019, where she got her first taste of apps rendering badly.

“Native apps could be slow to load, but brought the vision of a foldable future to life. Third-party apps — which were most of them — struggled to catch up quickly and smoothly to the demands of a folding screen,” Dolcourt said. “At the outset, some were barely usable.”

Nowadays, most apps are designed for Android foldables, in part thanks to years of Google software updates specifically addressing flexible displays. The Duo will have to play catch-up. 

But as Lanxon pointed out, Apple has deep relationships with developers of its apps, which sometimes launch on iOS first before heading to the Google Play Store. Apple will surely be working closely with its software partners to ensure they’re using the Duo’s proportions to the best advantage, Lanxon said. 

When your apps, like Instagram, will be updated to fit the Duo’s screens is hard to gauge (especially given it took 15 years to get an iPad-native Instagram app), but developers have many more advantages than they did when adapting to the first Android foldables’ displays. Over time — and hopefully soon — the Duo will be even better to use as apps catch up with it.  

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. As a true Californian, he lives for coffee, beaches and burritos.

title: iOS Decoded: iOS 27.2 RC – hands-on w/ HomePod Sound Glow, TV profiles, Apple TV Home Theater assets, more [Video]
snippet: In this episode of iOS Decoded, we take the HomePod’s new Sound Glow feature for a test drive and try out the new Lock Controls feature to prevent accidental activation of its top cap. fullText:
In this episode of iOS Decoded, we take the HomePod’s new Sound Glow feature for a test drive and try out the new Lock Controls feature to prevent accidental activation of its top cap.

We also go hands-on with other changes, like the handy new profiles option for the TV app and Suggested Actions for Messages. Further, we take a look at and listen to some of the assets and sounds from Apple TV’s new surround-sound Home Theater functionality.

Watch our full hands-on video as we dive into these changes and many more, and be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more.

Sound Glow

Starting with iOS 27.2, the HomePod mini and 2nd-generation HomePod will see their LED Matrix displays, which feature 19 and 37 RGB LEDs, respectively, used in a way they haven’t before, thanks to Sound Glow.

Sound Glow transforms the top cap into a color-matched animated visual canvas that matches the album artwork. The canvas glows and pulses in concert with the currently playing song or podcast, responding to changes in bass and treble. For Soundscape ambient sounds like rain, forest, fireplace, etc., bespoke RGB animations are used instead of the Sound Glow audio processing pipeline, since Soundscapes are very different from music.

Video: iOS 27.2 Top Features

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Users who have updated their iOS devices and HomePods to 27.2 will find a new Sound Glow toggle in the Home app under the HomePod settings.

I’ve tested Sound Glow fairly extensively, and I’ve been impressed by the feature. It gives music playback a slightly unique experience with each song. I’ve also been impressed by the sheer vibrancy of the display, as Apple is clearly making full use of all of the LEDs embedded under the top cap to generate unique colors based on the currently playing song.

Sound Glow is vibrant, but it’s not extremely bright, and won’t light up your room or anything. But if you place your HomePod in an area where the top cap is easily visible, it’s a really nice addition.

What’s more noteworthy is that Sound Glow isn’t just limited to new hardware like Apple’s recently announced HomePod mini 2. The feature also works with the first-generation HomePod mini and the second-generation full-sized HomePod. 

We’ve long known about the LED Matrix display that sits under the touch sensor, but it makes you wonder how long Apple has been sitting on such a feature internally, before deciding to announce it during the HomePod mini section of Apple’s recent HomeView hardware unveiling. My takeaway: Sound Glow may look simple on the surface, but there’s a lot of impressive engineering under the hood that generates these animations!

Lock Controls

Another new HomePod-focused feature found in iOS 27.2 is the ability to lock the touch surface to prevent both accidental and intentional interactions. Users will find a new Lock Controls toggle when opening the HomePod settings inside the Home app. Enabling this feature will disable touch interactions for touch, touch and hold, and volume controls.

When touching the top cap with Lock Controls enabled, you’ll see a red animation that shakes back and forth, as if it’s saying “no”. 

The red “no” indicator when using the touch panel with Lock Controls enabled

As I mentioned in the video walkthrough above, my cat sometimes paws at the top cap, causing the HomePod to play music. Enabling Lock Controls would eliminate that issue while still allowing human household members to control Siri by voice or via another iOS device.

In addition, Apple notes that Lock Controls will not interfere with the ability to interact with features such as timers, intercom alarms, check-in, or FaceTime calls via touch. All of those items will remain responsive to a touch of the top cap.

Apple TV Profiles

The TV app on iOS 27.2 now supports creating new profiles and switching between them, something we’ve already been using on tvOS. This feature is especially useful if you have small children who enjoy using your phone to watch content via the TV app. Now you can simply switch to your child’s profile, and they can enjoy their content without affecting your profile. In other words, no more episodes of Duck & Goose or Frog and Toad littering your Up Next queue.

TV app profiles come in handy when sharing your device with kids

Suggested Actions

The Suggested Actions feature for the Messages app first appeared in the initial iOS 27 betas but was eventually removed before iOS 27 shipped. Now, in iOS 27.2, Apple is ready to ship the feature that will automatically suggest actions based on what’s in your Messages thread. For example, if you paste an address, you might receive an Open in Maps suggestion, or if you type in a date, an Add to Calendar suggestion may appear.

Messages suggestions return for the first time since the iOS 27 beta

Users can fine-tune the types of suggestions presented in Settings → Messages → Suggested Actions. There, you can toggle on or off add to Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Show in Maps, and Flight and Packages suggestions. Apple also notes that suggestions that you don’t use will stop appearing after a month.

Apple TV Home Theater setup

We’ve discovered lots of interesting new assets that give us a behind-the-scenes look at the setup process for the fourth-generation Apple TV’s Home Theater capability, made possible by adding four HomePods in two separate stereo pairs.

A look at the different HomePod Home Theater configs with Apple TV 4th-generation

We also get a look at some of the animations used during that process, along with an impressive-sounding Celebration animation upon successfully calibrating your Home Theater. You can listen to the corresponding sound just below:

9to5Mac’s Take

These features are just the tip of the iceberg in terms of all that we uncovered in the iOS 27.2 beta. In our hands-on video, we discuss details about unreleased iPhone and iPad hardware we found. I let you hear and see lots of new sounds and assets from the HomeView setup process, and more. Stay tuned for future episodes of iOS Decoded, where we go deeper than the surface level in terms of new iOS releases!

title: iPhone Duo review roundup: The same problems Android foldables face, but with Apple’s polish
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth.

Ahead of the first shipments arriving for customers later this week, the avalanche of iPhone Duo reviews has arrived today and, with it, the first look at what it’s like to live with Apple’s first foldable. 

Starting with our sister site 9to5Mac, of course, Chance used the iPhone Duo for a week and walked away “convinced that this form factor represents the future of the iPhone.” His in-depth review hits on every key aspect of this device, but his ultimate conclusion boils down to this being the future of Apple’s smartphones because the form fact “just makes sense” and that there’s “something special about a compact, notebook-like iPhone that unfolds into a tablet-like experience.”

9to5Mac: iPhone Duo review: The future is foldable

Looking at iPhone Duo reviews from the perspective of someone who’s been using Android foldables as their daily driver for over half a decade at this point, I can’t help but look at Apple’s first attempt and see the foundation it’s building on, but also the places where Apple’s inherent polish comes into play.

	

One big part of that seems to be the inner display. The nanotexture matte finish sounds like a big deal, with it making the crease visually not a problem. It’s still there, Chance stresses in his 9to5Mac review, but you “almost never” notice it visually unless you’re looking for it – just like most Android foldables. He adds that you’re more likely to feel it than see it. 

The app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet. That’s what pushed Android foldables into the “phone that turns into a square tablet” trend they were stuck in for years, despite brands like Oppo and Google coming up with this iPhone Duo form factor way before Apple was a part of the conversation. Apple has the same problem, and it’s not going to be fixed overnight.

That said, it’s clear that it’s going to get cleaned up much quicker. WIRED‘s review opens up mentioning how “in the past day” key apps including “Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.”

“Mr Foldable” himself, Michael Fisher, explains in his review how apps that are not optimized are rough, comparing it to the early days of iPad, but that some key players are already stepping up. On top of that, smaller devs are building apps clearly inspired of this new form factor. “Tiny Computers” looks absolutely delightful.

David Imel mentions that “you can scale things up and they work, but they do look silly” in regards to unoptimized apps, and also makes a good point – not everything is going to get updated. iOS apps that aren’t actively maintained anymore are always going to be a mess on this device and, frankly, the scaling features Apple gives you make everything look way worse than an unoptimized app on an Android foldable has ever looked.

Look at the options you get for the yet-to-be-optimized Google Maps. Michael Fisher points out how it still doesn’t take up the whole display and that, if you rotate the phone, it just sends you back to square one. Sounds bad!

Apple’s new sidebar UI, which I still think looks funky, is personally my biggest fear as these wide foldable form factors take over, not because it’s a bad idea – Fisher points out that he actually loves it – but because Android apps will probably take a whole lot longer to adopt it. Seeing where things are starting out on the iPhone Duo, yeah, I’m sticking with that take.

That outer display, too, seems to be a hang up. The Verge says that “most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time.” That’s a problem I ran into a bit with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its similar shout and stout form factor, but Apple’s device is even smaller, so I’m not shocked to hear this. 

That same review makes a case for Apple’s app split, saying that “the problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time,” while saying that “the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them.” I’m not sure I agree there – larger canvases and multitasking alone have sold me on a foldable for years – but seeing so many iOS apps going all-in on the new screen size certainly has me feeling a bit envious. 

Another review that caught my eye was from Joanna Stern, where she puts the iPhone Duo “through hell.” There are two things of note here. First, Joanna puts the Duo through over 32,000 folds on top of normal daily use, and the hinge unsurprisingly holds up well. Android brands have laid an incredible foundation here, so even if Apple took its own route, the technology is clearly up to par here for a strong foldable hinge. 

But also pointed out here is a problem that’s been on every single Android foldable I’ve ever used – the iPhone Duo gets warm. Joanna calls the device a “hand warmer” and, apparently, Apple said this was business as usual for the device’s heat management. I was curious if the thicker design of Duo would help alleviate this one, but it seems Apple is dealing with the same issue. It’s a lot harder to cool two halves of a device, and you feel that heat more when there’s more usable space on the device.

Virtually every review mentions how hefty the iPhone Duo’s hardware is, too. This is a problem that Android foldables have been chipping away at generation-by-generation, and that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the poster child for. Smartphone weight continues to be something you don’t notice until it pushes over the edge and, while we’re not at Pixel Fold levels, iPhone Duo is very much at that edge.

Based on these early reviews, Apple didn’t reinvent the foldable, but it’s clear there’s a level of polish on the iPhone Duo that was lacking on Android foldables. Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start. 

What’s next for Android foldables? I look forward to seeing exactly that…

title: Leaker reveals larger iPhone Duo details, possible Telephoto camera
snippet: Today on Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the prolific leaker offered fresh insights into several features in the works for future iPhone Duo models, including larger screen sizes and possibly a Telephoto camera. more…
fullText:
Today on Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the prolific leaker offered fresh insights into several features in the works for future iPhone Duo models, including larger screen sizes and possibly a Telephoto camera.

Mark Gurman details Apple’s plans for larger iPhone Duo, says Telephoto is ‘on their list’ for future models

The iPhone Duo isn’t yet available in stores, but Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman already has plenty to share about Apple’s plans for future models.

Today on his Power On podcast, Gurman revealed that Apple is testing iPhone Duo 2 models with Face ID under the outer display, and is exploring ways to add an Action button. You can read more about those details here.

Later in the episode, Gurman looks further out to a 2028 third-gen model that he’s previously reported on.

The iPhone Duo 3 is expected to be slightly larger, and on the podcast Gurman offered specifics on what to expect. He said:

What I heard, just to be specific about the larger screen version of the Duo, is I heard…it’s marginal. It would be that the bigger screen, or the inside screen, increasing by, it’s like, this is rough, like very roughly half an inch. And so, that wouldn’t necessarily make the outer screen much bigger…we’re not talking about an 8.5-inch, 9-inch inner screen. We’re talking about like high sevens, very low eights.

For reference, iPhone Duo currently has a 7.6-inch folding display.

	

Gurman compares the forthcoming change to how Apple gradually sized up its Pro line in recent years. For example, it went from 6.7 inches on iPhone 15 Pro Max to 6.9 inches on iPhone 16 Pro Max.

As part of the conversation, Gurman is also asked if Apple is going to add a Telephoto camera to a future iPhone Duo. He says, “That’s on their list. I don’t know when that’s coming, but that’s gonna be hard to do.” 

He adds that it isn’t a matter of cost, but physics: “I think that’s purely a physics issue in terms of the depth needed. It’s going to be interesting to see how they end up solving that.”

Would you want a slightly larger iPhone Duo, and how important is a Telephoto lens to you? Let us know in the comments.

title: YouTube Is Letting Us Vibe Our Video Feeds, and I’m Liking It
snippet: The mobile app is giving users more control of the videos they get.
fullText:
Let’s face it — we love scrolling through videos. Maybe you’re OK with what YouTube feeds you, maybe you’re not. Either way, you’ve now got more control over it.

YouTube this week added a feature to the mobile app home page that enables you to create your own video feeds for whatever topics you want. The feed helps you home in on the subjects that appeal to you instead of necessarily relying on the algorithm. The custom feed option appears as a plus sign on the horizontal menu at the top of the app’s home screen.

YouTube said in its announcement that it wants to help users “dive straight into” their favorite content. “We know that viewers come to YouTube with incredibly unique interests, moods, topics to explore, and favorite ways to watch,” the YouTube team said.

			

More from CNET

The horizontal menu is also new. It includes tabs for your custom feeds, subscribed channels, music and live streams. There’s also a Music & TV button for people who subscribe to YouTube TV or Primetime Channels.

To see it for yourself, go to the app’s home screen on your phone. At the top, you’ll see the menu. If you click on Subs, you’ll see your subscribed channels. The Music tab will show videos from your favorite artists, and the Live button will show livestreams from your favorite creators. The More button shows a menu of YouTube features.

Trying out the new YouTube settings

But the most intriguing addition was the custom feed feature, and I gave it a go. On the YouTube home screen menu, I clicked on the plus sign. Then, under the “Add a custom feed for any topic or mood,” I typed San Francisco 49ers, and voila, a new tab appeared on the menu — SF 49ers. I also added a feed for the 2026 midterm elections. Both of those feeds now appear in the menu.

You can create a YouTube video feed for any topic.YouTube

You can also modify or delete a feed. If you click into a feed, you’ll see buttons at the top to edit the prompt, rename the feed or delete the feed.

I decided to modify my 49ers feed. Since I’m also a fan of the Golden State Warriors NBA team, I changed the feed topic to include both the 49ers and the Warriors. That feed then showed videos for both teams.

For non-Premium users, you get three feeds. You get up to eight if you subscribe to YouTube Premium ($9 per month).

The custom feed feature was already available on desktop — added by YouTube last month. It’s not yet available on tablets, and YouTube owner Google hasn’t said when it will be.

You must be 13 or older to get the custom feeds feature, and you also must have both watch and search history enabled.

title: You should pick up this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL over its $1,300 sequel
snippet: Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon. more…
fullText:
Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon.

It’s no secret that consumer tech prices are continuing to balloon in the face of AI-driven RAM shortages, which makes any deal on last-gen tech always worth considering. It says a lot that, even removed from that context, this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL in Moonstone remains an all-around great deal, saving you a whopping $450 over its successor without much in the way of meaningful sacrifices. In fact, considering the 256GB variant actually has more RAM than this year’s base Pro XL model, you might come out ahead in the long run.

Buy Pixel 10 Pro XL for $850 at Amazon

Still, it’s worth breaking some of those sacrifices down. In addition to the obvious downside of losing a year’s worth of software upgrades — since we’re a full 12 months further along the Pixel 10’s seven-year lifecycle — you’ll have to be willing to lose a handful of changes on both the hardware and software fronts. Other hardware changes include a Tensor G5 over the G6, a slightly dimmer display, a smaller telephoto sensor, and, of course, the lack of everybody’s favorite underbaked Google feature, HiLight.

But hey, at least you get a temperature sensor and a brighter flash.

On the software side, Camera Looks is the big missing tool, with no plans to bring my favorite Pixel camera feature to previous generations on the horizon. However, I wouldn’t say Camera Looks is worth the extra $450, especially when Camera Looks being backported certainly remains a possibility in play. The same goes for Google’s typical slate of AI features; tools like Rambler remain Pixel 11-exclusive for now, but considering third-party developers have already made their own moves in this regard, I would expect to see an improved take on the company’s latest voice-to-text model show up sooner rather than later.

	

Don’t sleep on this deal; we’ve already seen a $700 sale price for the smaller Pixel 10 Pro in 256GB sell out (though the 128GB model is still available for $750). If you’re looking for a new phone to help you weather RAMageddon — and you don’t want to break the bank to buy it — this Pixel 10 Pro XL might be your best hope.

Google TV is rolling out its latest feature roundup, showcasing new features and additions that have rolled out in recent months.

Gemini-aided “Remix your photos”

Dynamic slideshows

title: Apple exploring fix for Safari’s cramped layout on the iPhone Duo’s outer display
snippet: In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details.

Apple knows Safari isn’t making full use of iPhone Duo’s outer display

One issue singled out in multiple iPhone Duo reviews (including ours) was the fact that Safari’s right-aligned controls take up a significant portion of the outer display’s limited screen space, leaving websites with an unusually narrow area to show their content.

Here’s what Chance Miller had to say about this in his review, published earlier this week:

But the awkwardness of the iPhone’s 5.4-inch outer display shows up in Safari. The web simply isn’t optimized for this form factor. I’ll talk more about this later, but the right-aligned controls on iPhone Duo eat into the usable screen real estate in Safari especially.

[…]

I can see why Apple chose the design it did for Safari on the iPhone Duo. I don’t think overlapping the controls with the website would’ve made sense. Still, scrolling in Safari is one of the best examples of something that’s better on the inner screen.

For new iPhone Duo users who have also been frustrated by this issue, Apple’s Jen Simmons shared some good news today.

In a post highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, including how websites adapt to the iPhone Duo’s different screen sizes and folding positions, Simmons acknowledged that websites currently can’t extend behind the controls on the device’s outer display, and said Apple is exploring ways to address that limitation.

From her post:

We would like to give web designers and developers the ability to design and use that space in more creative ways. Perhaps you want to extend your header background across the full width of the display, for example. It might seem like there’s just one obvious way to make this possible, but really there are many possibilities.

Simmons went on to explain that simply using the HTML viewport meta tag with viewport-fit="cover" to extend websites behind Safari’s controls could cause problems, because many websites don’t properly account for those areas, potentially leaving important content obscured.

Instead, she invited developers to share their ideas as Apple explores a better approach:

We are investigating if there’s a better way to accomplish the same result — something more foolproof and perhaps easier for you to use. If you have ideas, we’d love to hear them. And stay tuned.

If you’re a web developer and have ideas on how Apple could address this limitation, you can read the full WebKit post for details on how to share your feedback.

title: Man Destroys $2,000 iPhone Duo With Dirt, Fire, Knives and Medieval Chainmail
snippet: YouTuber JerryRigEverything tests the iPhone Duo’s durability for scratch and dust resistance. And it is wild to watch.
fullText:
It might seem obvious, but try not to sit on your iPhone Duo when you leave it open.

That lesson comes a day after Apple’s foldable iPhone hit stores with lines of people queued up to buy the new device. Tech reviewer Zach Nelson dropped an iPhone Duo video on his YouTube channel, JerryRigEverything, testing the scratch resistance and bendability of the new $2,000 phone. 

Let’s just say that Nelson’s measured, soothing voice didn’t keep me calm as he meticulously destroyed the Duo.

			

More from CNET

He subjected it to numerous scratch tests on both its cover and inner screens. Nelson praised Apple for the cover screen’s Ceramic Shield 2 glass and noted that the inner screen, even with its nano-texture finish, scratches as easily as the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s nonmatte folding display.

But why stop there?

Nelson used medieval chainmail (no proof it was actually from the Middle Ages), dirt, dust and pebbles to test the Duo further. Surprisingly, the new phone handled the chainmail easily. Nelson partly credits that to the Duo’s matte finish on the inner screen, which seems to hide imperfections. 

He then opened the Duo’s inner screen and tried to bend it backward a few times. As you might expect, the frame flexed, which led to cracks showing up on the main 7.6-inch screen. So if you set your Duo down with its main screen open on a chair or couch, just don’t sit on it.

In a review by CNET senior technology reporter Abrar Al-Heeti, Al-Heeti recommends protecting the Duo, saying, “You should probably still get a case and AppleCare, or be prepared to pay a pretty penny for repairs.”

You can watch Nelson’s video to see the entire nearly 15-minute video. Warning: the dust and dirt portion against the Duo’s hinge is psychologically difficult to witness (because of all the dust and dirt). Also, if you’re wondering more about the iPhone Duo’s durability, CNET has designed and constructed a custom machine called the Fold-a-Phone that is currently hard at work testing how many times Apple’s foldable can be open and closed.

title: Gemini Notebook now available as Connected App for deeper integration
snippet: Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration. more…
fullText:
Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration.

As a Connected App like Google Workspace or Photos, @Gemini Notebook “allows you to manage and query notebooks directly within your chats using natural language.”

This integration lets you retrieve information from existing notebooks, create new ones, add sources, and save notes. The Gemini app will “automatically detect when to use the Gemini Notebook Connected App for relevant prompts.” For example: 

Create, edit, or delete a notebook (“Create a Gemini Notebook about solar farm market trends”)

Add, update, or delete sources in a notebook (“Add a copy of this chat to my notebook about Bio 101 course”)

List notebooks and their sources (“Show me a list of all the sources in my notebook about US National Parks”)

Answer questions using context from your notebook (“What do my Gemini Notebooks say about butterfly migration?”)

This integration is available now and has been enabled by “default for users globally, except in the European Economic Area, where it will be OFF by default.”

	

@Gemini Notebook is “available to all Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and users with personal Google accounts.”

title: Kevin Roose is AGI-pilled. Why aren’t you?
snippet: Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry. Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork, but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods, which launched last week. Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence. I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth. Okay: Kevin Roose on The AGI Chronicles, starting Machine Gods, and where AI goes from here. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Kevin Roose, you are the author of The AGI Chronicles and the cofounder and co-host of the new podcast Machine Gods. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much for having me. I was listening to the first episode of Machine Gods and you and Casey discussed the fact that technically you have the title of CEO. It’s true. I won the coin flip and we needed someone. When you start a company as we have, you need to list someone as the CEO, I guess, to know who to haul in front of Congress when our first scandal inevitably breaks. So that’s going to be me. It’s funny because you’re a CEO on Decoder. It means I’m going to have to ask you the Decoder questions. [Laughs] Okay. Well, I’ve been a CEO for about five minutes and most days I frankly forget I’m the CEO. Honestly, that tracks with most of the CEOs on the show. They all act like they’ve only done it for five minutes. We’ll come to it. I want to talk about your book. It’s called The AGI Chronicles. It is a meticulously reported book about the main frontier labs and the culture shift they’ve all undergone as AI has come into the forefront and become a much more commercial product in many ways. But let’s just start with Machine Gods. You were a journalist for The New York Times for a long time. Obviously, I think the audience probably knows this, but you and I have known each other for a long time. I will say that since I have known you, your desire to be a YouTuber has been top of mind. You’re just like, “How do I get over there?” And I’ve always been like, “Run, don’t do it.” But you did it. You left The Times, you started your own podcast with our friend Casey Newton. It is the next generation of the very popular podcast, Hard Fork, which was excellent. And I’m excited for you, but what made you take the leap? Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Yeah, you have been trying to convince me out of this for as long as I’ve been trying to convince myself into it and you have not succeeded because here I am. Yep, I failed. Utterly failed. No, look, I think that for some very good reasons, media companies have long been a little bit wary of going all in on YouTube or any other video platform. The ones that have gone all in have not necessarily come out of that with good feelings about it because there are a lot of– Yeah, they pivot to video and also into death, routinely. Yeah, you pivot to video or you sort of waste a bunch of money doing things that don’t pay for themselves. So, I think there are some structural economic reasons for that, but I also think it’s that there aren’t a lot of institutions that are equipped to make that kind of a long-term bet. I’ve been trying to YouTube-pill people in media for many years, as you know. You’ve been trying to undo the YouTube-pilling on your end, but I just think it’s clearly the most important media platform in the world right now. It’s a place where journalism has not historically had a central place. If you were to look at YouTube as a whole and try to assess what piece of it is dedicated to what you or I would consider high-quality journalism, it’s a vanishingly small part of the overall ecosystem there. So, part of my mission is just to crack that and figure out how to do YouTube and video in general in a way that is sustainable from an economic and a sort of creative standpoint. And then just to experiment and do a bunch of things. This is not a face that needs to be on YouTube. So I’m also hoping to bring some other people in and nail some formats. But I look at what The Verge has done there. I look at what people like Joanna Stern and MKBHD have done there. To me, that is very exciting and it’s a space where there’s a lot less competition than text or podcasts. Machine Gods is a podcast that you’re doing in partnership with NPR, which I want to talk about. But do you think of it as a YouTube product? We want it to be video-first. What that means basically is that we are going to give a shit about what it looks like to a degree that we have not always done. We’re going to try to give people a lot of reasons to want to watch as well as listen. Obviously, we know that there are some people who just don’t like video podcasts and so we want to give the audio audience something that is enjoyable, but this is the direction of things. You can’t do a podcast now without doing video on top of it. So we’re going to try to really embrace that and make a good version of it that is as good as two middle-aged journalists can pull off on YouTube. Truly the future of media is middle-aged journalists pivoting to YouTube. I feel the same way because I’m now making more video and that’s what we’re doing. It’s going to be great. The other reason to leave and to do this — and obviously people know I’m friends with Casey as well, and I’ve been talking to you and him about it for a long time — is that the AI story is here. There is a platform shift. There are new companies, new characters, new ideas to talk about in the world. It’s funny because in that context, usually you get a media shift as well. The way we tell stories or the formats we tell stories usually shifts alongside the thing we are talking about or the technology we’re talking about. Here, YouTube feels like the most solid media foundation that exists. It’s the one that’s the same the most, even though it’s changing and it has YouTube Shorts and now you can A/B test everything, including your own face. But it’s the one that is the most the same. Instagram has undergone some massive change and it feels like that will continue happening. Does it feel like YouTube is the most stable place to build as you’re trying to tell these new stories? It does. I mean, obviously you never want to put all your eggs in one basket. So, we are also distributing video on Apple Podcasts and Spotify and we’re going to be everywhere. But yeah, it feels relatively stable. The question I’m always wondering is what would it take to replace YouTube?
