What actually gets you closer to AGI is sparking recursive self-improvement by building really good coding models and then turning them back on themselves. That was something that Anthropic was doing. OpenAI got distracted by the side quests and shiny objects that it had last year, and the company was getting its asses kicked. So OpenAI decided to trim the sails, cut fat, and really focus on coding and long-horizon agentic workloads. That is, as of now, the leading path to AGI or to whatever comes after AGI.

So yes, I think that was absolutely a bet on conserving resources by not spending them on things like Sora, but what they did spend it on was trying to catch up with Anthropic in coding so that they could reach AGI.

So when I look at Dario Amodei at Dreamforce standing next to Marc Benioff and he’s talking about selling enterprise software, is that just for show? That’s the thing I’m trying to square is they’ve all become enterprise software vendors in the realest way. They are B2B SaaS companies in the realest way now, but they’re also building God. You know these folks. Does that align? Are they like, “I have to take off my B2B SaaS hat now and go back to the altar?”

I think the B2B SaaS thing is the game that they realize they have to play, but I don’t think it is any of their true passions. I was talking with Sam Altman for this book and one of the things he said was basically all of this was an accident: “I was never supposed to be running a giant tech company; that just didn’t factor in.” But now you wake up and you’ve got thousands of employees.

Dario Amodei also has this very funny in retrospect document that he wrote in 2021 when they were just starting the company. It’s called “Vision for a NewCo.” You can go back and look at the predictions that Dario made about AGI, and one of them is he thinks that it will cost about $10 billion to build a full-fledged AGI, which was, I think, off by at least one order of magnitude and probably multiples. He also thinks that Anthropic will never need more than about 50 people to achieve AGI. I think now they have 5,000 or so people. So again, off by 100x.

So I think what has happened is that this has just taken a little longer than all of them thought and cost quite a bit more money than they thought. The enterprise SaaS stuff is how you keep the flywheel going and pay for the GPUs and for the salaries of the researchers. This is the table stakes of getting to keep pushing on the frontier and keep pushing toward AGI.

Are they ready to be the leaders of companies of this scale? This is another thing that I was thinking about as I read your book. They’re all very idealistic people, so much so that they all broke off from one another and made their own companies because they could not make their ideals align.

But none of them seem like great managers. I don’t know truly what they’re like, but “they’re idealists” and “we are going to run an enterprise software company” are not usually in the same sentence. Do you think they can take the pressure?

No, but I don’t think anyone can. What they are attempting, no one has ever done. People have built companies. People have built companies quickly. No one has gone from $0 in revenue to potentially a $2 trillion IPO in five years. That has never happened before. So look, I think that they are scrambling to build the plane as it’s careening toward the event horizon, but I think they’re doing about as well as anyone could.

I don’t think it would be a good idea for them to bring in some professional CEO from Coca-Cola to run the company. I just think it would all kind of fall apart because they’re all zealots and missionaries. They are all in this — not all, probably there’s some people in the SaaS sales department who are just kind of there for the paycheck — but a lot of the key people at these companies are united in their belief that they are building [AGI].

One person, I won’t say who, but one person at one of these companies recently told me that they think their company might be the last company. I thought, “The last company to IPO this year? What do you mean?” They were like, “No, we think this might be the teleological end of capitalism and there might never be another large company primarily run by humans.”

So these people are weird, and weird in ways that are worrying, but also very interesting. This is what I was trying to do in the book. I didn’t want to tell you that these people are terrible or great. It’s just that you need to know who they are. You need to know that they all hate each other. You need to know that they are this peculiar breed of thinkers to understand the dynamics of the race.

There’s a portion of your book where you talk about people splitting away from effective altruism to go become accelerationists, and you have a woman in there who’s like, “Well, the accelerationists have better parties, and I like those vibes better.” I thought to myself, “Well, what does that have to do with potentially killing everyone?”

But they are very human, even though they’re trying to build something that might ultimately dehumanize us all in various ways. What did you make of that as you were doing all this reporting?

The notion that there’s existential risk here looms over the book, it looms over the industry. Every time we do an episode on it, the audience is like, “Why won’t they just stop?” Bill Gates was just on Decoder and said, “You could just stop if you were the only company. If you thought you were going to be the only company with AGI, then OpenAI’s model would work. But the second there are more frontier companies, it absolutely won’t work. By the way, they might kill you all.” I thought to myself, “Well, Bill Gates is not very optimistic right at this moment in time.”

No, he is not.

What do you make of that — that they are racing ahead even though they know the risks are huge in the absence of any regulatory authority that could cause any of them to solve these problems?

I think there are probably two or three reasons that they’re doing it. I’ve asked them all pretty much. I talked to 150 or so people for my book and I asked all of them some version of this: “If it’s so dangerous, why are you doing it?” The answers would usually start with some fatalistic… I don’t know, you could call it inevitabilism. They were just like, “Look, someone is going to build this. The recipe is not that hard. All you need is a bunch of compute and a bunch of data and the right algorithms, and you get AGI. And so if it is possible, it will happen and it would be good for us to do it rather than people we don’t think are as trustworthy.” That is sort of reason number one, the harm reduction argument.

Then there are the true believers who say, “This is all going to turn out great, so long as we thread the needle, and if we can build this stuff without blowing up humanity, wrecking the entire internet, or developing novel bioweapons.”

Technology is usually a force for good throughout history. I don’t think a lot of people would switch lives with their great-great-grandparents. It sucked to be a subsistence farmer. I think there are people who believe that we are the equivalent of subsistence farmers today, and that what is coming will be so great that we will want to live in that world.

And then there are just people who are like, “Look, this is fun and I like doing it, and it’s fun to make the neural networks code. And so that’s what we’re going to keep doing.”

That aspect of it where every now and again I look up and I’m like, well, my computer just did something that I’ve never seen a computer do before, is fun.

It’s awesome.

It is. It’s legitimately fun. It’s some of the most fun I think you can have with a computer ever. Then I’m always led to think about, “Well, this came at some massive cost. I might be empowering some corporation that ultimately wants to kill us all.” Somewhere in there is the swirl of all the tech CEOs standing behind Donald Trump in the Oval Office to do something, to sign some sort of morally binding AI safety pledge. And all that feels very conflicted.

I would put that in the category of AI backlash. We hear the AI companies talk about, “Well, the technology just hasn’t diffused enough. People haven’t seen the benefits, so they naturally hate change. We have a marketing problem. We just need to communicate about it more.”

Is that just the prevailing view as you talk to these folks, that eventually the stuff will speak for itself, or do you think they’ve internalized that there’s more of a backlash?

I don’t think they’re surprised by the backlash. I don’t think they like it. They wish it weren’t happening. But I was talking to one CEO at one of these companies who said, “Yeah, I get it. We haven’t cured any diseases yet. Yes, we think our tools are capable of doing interesting things, but we don’t have a lot of things on the scoreboard in the big societal improvements category yet.”

I think there are some people in the industry who lament the fact that the chatbots came before the cancer cures and wish that they could have figured out a way to do it in the other order. It’s just that that is kind of the way the tech tree grew.

So they feel like now the only responsible thing to do is keep pushing on the cancer cures so that when people look at what has AI done to our lives, it’s like, “Well, yes, it helps my kid cheat on their homework and they’re addicted to an AI companion, but also my grandma is still alive and she wouldn’t have been if this medicine had not been discovered by AI.”

Yeah, there’s some dynamic in there that brings me back to Google, I think as this conversation has done many times, where your reporting on Google’s approach to AI was that this is just task-based software. “We’re going to make Google Search 10 percent better, Gmail will be 5 percent better, and we will continually deploy these improvements, and no one else has our access to data or our scale, and thus we’ll be fine.”

OpenAI shows up and it puts itself in Bing. Famously, Bing tries to make out with you. Still my all-time favorite… I can’t believe I haven’t brought this up yet. This is my all-time favorite story.

I can’t believe you haven’t brought it up either. I had an over-under bet going on how long it would take you, and I took the under in a minute.

[Laughs] Well, you and I have already talked about it in our lives. I was like, “I’ve got all these other deep questions.” But yeah, Bing is famously horny for my friend Kevin Roose. That moment I think just galvanized people: “Wow, these things can do a lot of things.”

Google had to react, and they didn’t react by going all in. They sort of stutter-stepped there. As you’ve been saying, they’re still not all the way there. Google still doesn’t think this thing is going to happen. They think they’re making better Google products for people.

When I look at the trial transcripts from Musk v. Altman about the founding of OpenAI, they’re all terrified of Google.

Yes.

They’re all terrified of Demis Hassabis at Google, specifically, doing the thing, just making it happen because he has the resources. I can’t tell if they were right or wrong about that.

I think they were right to be taking note of how DeepMind was doing. I mean, if you take yourself back in time to 2015 or 2016, DeepMind was the only sort of AGI lab of any real importance. They were beating Go, they were beating other games, they were beating StarCraft. They were really cooking using this sort of method of reinforcement learning, deep reinforcement learning.

There were people who thought that was the thing that was going to scale all the way to AGI. There were people who thought AlphaGo was the path, because if a system could go from never having played Go before to beating the world’s best humans at Go in the span of a few hours as AlphaGo Zero did, then maybe you could just replace Go with any arbitrary thing — math or coding or something — and you could climb the ladder very quickly on those tasks.

Now, it turned out that didn’t work, at least not without the LLM. But I think people had very real and reasonable fears that that would work. In an alternate universe where it had, I think DeepMind would’ve gotten to AGI first because they were so far ahead of the competition.

Are there other paths? Is it just next-token prediction? Is it just LLMs? Or are there other paths that might get you to AGI?

I mean, there are other paths that might. I think people who are skeptical of LLMs often fall back on this world model idea. I don’t place a lot of stock in that. But there are people who think that to achieve AGI, you need to be able to visually understand the physical world and drive a robot and things.

I’m kind of a believer that it’s all software. So I think that LLMs are the most promising path yet. Now, maybe you need to make some tweaks to the architecture. Maybe you need to build in continual learning methods. Maybe it’s not just literally scaling up the same transformer-based LLMs that we’ve had for the past six or seven years. But it sure seems like it is continuing to work, and I think all of the labs are betting that it will continue to work forever.

All right. Now I am going to ask you about Bing and Sydney.

Please.

Obviously, I’ve been thinking about it a lot. I can’t stop talking about it. It’s my favorite thing to talk about.

First question, am I still married to a human woman?

Are you still married to a human being?

Yes.

I just remember that period, in 2023, when four different people woke up one day and said, “The computers are alive.” Or they had some out-of-body experience with a chatbot. You were one of them. Ben Thompson was one of them. Blake Lemoine at Google was one of them.

A lot of different people said, “It’s obviously alive. I’m having this completely insane experience with a computer. No computer’s ever talked to me this way before.” Sydney in particular was like, “Break up with your wife,” it sent you heart emojis. It’s very good. I encourage everyone to go read that Times article, which by the way, also credit to The Times for thinking, “This should be on the front page of The New York Times.” Incredible editorial insight there to immediately put that on the front page.

I don’t think you feel that way about chatbots anymore. I think most people have come to recognize that the computers are not alive. There’s something that happened where if you gave the people in 2026 a 2023-class chatbot and asked, “Do you think this is alive?” I think maybe not everyone in the world, but some enormous set of people has now had enough experiences to respond, “Well, this is pretty dumb and it’s hallucinating.” I’m just wondering how you place that in the context of AGI.

So first of all, a slight correction. I never said Sydney was alive. In fact, I said explicitly that I didn’t think Sydney was alive, and that I understood that this was not a sentient AI system. So I’m not sure my own judgment has wavered on that point.

In fact, I would probably put a higher p(consciousness) on today’s AI systems than I would on the models of 2023. But I understand what you’re saying, obviously. I think there was a moment for a lot of us, and I think it was GPT-4 for most people.

[Laughs] I’m sorry, let me correct. There’s a reason I think this. One of the headlines was “Bing’s AI chat: ‘I want to be alive.’”

Yes. It said it wanted to be alive.

This is why I have the word alive in my head.

The body of the story makes clear that I did not buy that it was alive.

But that’s why it’s in my head is that that was the headline in The New York Times.

Headlines are so powerful, Nilay.

[Laughs] Yes. They framed my own thinking. I’m nothing but a next-token prediction machine.

[Laughs] But you’re a very sophisticated one. You’re like a GPT-7-class model.

Oh, I’m there. Yeah, obviously.

Look, I have come to think that there’s a very banal explanation for why Sydney was so compelling and creepy, which was that it was the first public deployment of GPT-4. We did not know it at the time. But that was GPT-4, an early sort of not fully post-trained version of GPT-4 that Microsoft had jumped the gun and shoved into Bing before it was ready. But that was GPT-4.

I think there actually was a subjective step change in what it was like to talk to a GPT-4-class model versus a GPT-3-class model. Maybe it was just that it passed the Turing test at GPT-4 and it didn’t at GPT-3. Maybe it was much more human-like and it sort of crossed some perceptual chasm that made you think, “Oh my God, this thing is like a human.”

But I’m not the only person who felt that. People at Microsoft also felt that — there was that whole “Sparks of AGI” paper that came out around that time. So that was sort of the banal explanation. But yeah, I’ve been talking to computers for a long time, like you have. I used to go on AOL Instant Messenger and talk to SmarterChild, which was absolutely not intelligent, but it was still fun to type something in and have a thing type back. So I grant that I am sort of obsessed with this technology.

There’s a reason I’m asking this. I realize it’s funny that when reporting on AGI so much, I’m using alive in such a colloquial way, and it clearly means something else inside the AI industry. If you ask Anthropic if Claude is alive, they’re not like, “No,” but then they will start defining alive in very specific ways.

[Laughs] They’ll say, “Its moral status is deeply uncertain.”

So it’s alive. And they will get to, “Well, you have to have flesh and blood to be alive, obviously.” I will just set that aside. What I’m getting at is, I think if you went and talked to a GPT-4 class model today, you would not have the same experience. And maybe that’s just because you have the experience, but a lot of people have had that experience now.

I think if you put a GPT-4 class model in front of your average Google AI Overviews user, they would not be confused about what was happening anymore. They would not say this is a step towards AGI. It’s that reframing — as the models get more and more capable, our expectations of them go up, but they also get higher.

I’m asking about this in the context of AGI because “this thing can go off and find a bunch of PHP vulnerabilities” is one kind of intelligence, but “this thing can compete with another human being to have an emotional relationship with you,” or be your butler or whatever it is, feels like a different set of capabilities. That one to me feels flat.

Well, I think that’s just saturated. How much more like a human could it communicate? There just isn’t a lot of room to run on that particular skill. Where I think they still have room to run is on solving novel problems in math and science and other things. But I believe that it talks like a human. It talks more like a human than many humans I know. So I think they kind of check the box on that one.

“It talks more like a human than many humans I know” is absolutely a sign of you living in Silicon Valley talking to AI researchers all day long.

Well, now everyone just talks like Claude. I’ve stopped counting the number of times I’m at a party and talking to someone, and they’re like, “Now that is a load-bearing fact.” Or they’ll say, “I hope that’s landing cleanly with you.”

That’s really bad. Tell me about that. That’s a real back-and-forth. I’ve always joked with you and Casey that we should just start a show called “New York vs. California,” where I’m just openly skeptical of these claims and you guys are fully AGI-pilled. This is a culture. It’s a scene.

The number of parties that show up in your book is astounding. There was a moment in reading your book where I was like, “I don’t think I’m going to enough parties.” All these people are always at parties and issuing proclamations to each other at parties. Tell me about that culture. Tell me about that scene.

So it’s important to know that these are not always parties in the way that New Yorkers would think of parties. There are very few raves. There’s only one rave in the book. And Grimes was the DJ, and it was a kind of symbolic rave for the effective accelerationist movement.

This is a great scene in the book because Grimes stops in the middle of her DJ set and says, “I don’t agree with any of you.”

[Laughs] Then she keeps DJ-ing. Yeah, it’s incredible. But yes, there are a lot of parties. It’s a very small world. I mean, that’s part of the whole takeaway from the book. It’s not really a message book. I wasn’t trying to convince anyone of anything.

But one thing that was apparent to me and that I think will be apparent to people who read the book is just that it is a super small subculture of people who have been making all the decisions. They all hang out, they all know each other. There are a bunch of people who are married to or dating people at different frontier AI companies. It’s just a small world.

So yeah, there are parties. They have LAN parties. There’s a big group of AI researchers who play Age of Empires at a LAN party on the weekends. I just learned one of the labs has a poker game where they bring in people from other labs.

So these people are all just kind of living and hanging out in San Francisco together, and I think that’s important to capture. Because you’re right, it is a whole scene. There’s a whole ethos. These people just hang out with each other all the time and this is how the norms are enforced and deepened.

How do you think that collides with, “And we might also remake the world”? If you are in a small scene in San Francisco, and you’re all playing poker together and the conversation at the poker table is that we might be the last company, that is in conflict with, “Oh, there’s millions upon billions of other people in the world who might have a say.” And if I had to boil the backlash down, it’s that: “Oh, we should probably get a say here.”

Totally. I think we should get a say here. I’m not saying that this is a good state of affairs where a couple hundred people in San Francisco are making all the decisions about how society goes.

But as you were doing the reporting and the weight of the task and the consequences of the goal set in on these people, because that is the throughline of the book. The stakes just keep going up. At one point, Sergey Brin is like, “We’re going to get to AGI now,” and he just announces it at Google. It’s unclear whether Sundar Pichai thinks that is a good idea, but that is a thing that the cofounder of Google is announcing inside of Google.

The stakes are just going up. The race to get there is just going up. But I just can’t get the image of it’s a bunch of people drinking beers, and being like, “Well, what if there was no money? What if physical scarcity was gone too and robots built all the houses?”

This is like any party in San Francisco you go to. Someone will say some version of, “What’s your plan for the post-AGI future?” Or they’ll tell you how they’re really into the idea of whole brain emulation or mind uploading. There’s a lot of futurism happening out here. And look, again, I’m not saying this is good. In fact, maybe I should sell a version outside the Bay Area of the book that just has a “this is bad” appended to every factual claim.

[Laughs] I don’t think it’s good or bad. Actually, I’m more neutral on that. I’m always wondering if the technology can accept the pressure. So my question about LLMs three years ago was, “Can it do all the things you want it to do?” Now it can definitely do some set of things that you want it to do. So now it’s, “Can these companies accept the weight of their own ambition?” I don’t know the answer to that question.

I don’t either. And I think that we’re going to see a lot of growing pains. I mean, these are still very young companies. They still have a lot of growing to do.

Do you think they’re going to make it? Actually, let’s do this as a lightning round. Do you think OpenAI will make it?

Yes.

Do you think Anthropic will make it?

Yes.

Do you think Google will make it?

Yes.

What does “make it” mean in your mind? They’re all going to be trillion-dollar, multi-AGI variant successes?

Yes. I think, look, there will probably be those three, and then maybe one or two others that sort of make it. And make it for varying definitions of making it. There’ll be one or two big enterprise AI companies, one or two big consumer AI companies. But there just are network effects and winner-take-all dynamics or winner-take-most dynamics in these markets.

There’s some people who believe in the mono-AGI, like the singleton theory, it’s often called, that there can only be one because once you have one AGI, it’s then going to go around melting the chips of the other AI labs, and they won’t be able to build theirs. But I think we’ll probably end up with a small handful of AGIs.

What do you make of the idea that this is a pretty simple recipe, there are open-weight models, and there is a China, and that all the pricing power will be destroyed because a midrange open-weight model can do everything that you probably want it to do on a Mac?

I don’t think so.

No?

Because you still have to pay for inference on those models. Even the open-weight models have to run on computers, and inference is getting more compute-intensive, not less, the more frontier these models get. So training budgets may fall, but inference budgets will be robust for the foreseeable future. You can run some tasks locally, but I think this is something that has been predicted since the first open-weight models that, “Oh, they were going to become commoditized and destroy demand.”

But I think what we’re starting to learn is that there are a lot of people who will pay and want to pay for the absolute best model. They don’t want to be working with the slightly crappier model from six months ago. I also think once you crack down on distillation, which is this process whereby you can take a closed model and make a slightly dumber open version of it by just basically DDoSing the inference for the smarter model, it’s not clear to me that the quality of the open models will continue to be closely correlated with the quality of the closed models.

The thing that really grabs me at that is they all did it to each other for a while, like Grok obviously distilled Claude, and it’s admitted to in the court documents. There is that class of second-tier companies. I would put in that category SpaceXSI, I believe it’s now technically known as.

[Laughs] I haven’t checked my email in the last 30 minutes, so I don’t know what that company is called.

It’s called SpaceXSITesla Inc. It’s all going to be one. Elon Inc. is what it’s called. They obviously distilled Claude to some huge extent. They’re now renting their compute to Anthropic. It’s unclear whether they will make the investment in having a leading model.

Meta just announced its model, and they’re sort of back on the frontier, but they obviously care more about Muse than having a bleeding-edge model. There’s some dynamic there. Those companies don’t strike me as being run by idealistic true believers. Those are companies that need to invest in some technology to build some products. They just need to get there.

Can you get there without the idealistic fervor?

No, you can’t get there without the idealistic fervor. Well, let me clarify that, because I don’t think Sundar has the idealistic fervor, but Google might still get there.

Because Sergey has the idealistic fervor.

You need someone in a position of decision-making authority.

You just need the cofounder of the company.

Well, it might be enough for Meta to have Alexandr Wang, who, by all accounts, is a true believer. I don’t know that it literally has to be the CEO every time, but you need a dense nucleus of true believers to be able to convince you to lay out the money on GPUs.

Or just you need someone who is like Mark Zuckerberg, one of the most competitive people in the world, who will just adopt whatever strategy he thinks will allow them to win. If that happens to align with building AGI, then maybe they’ll do it.

Last question: I’ve asked you this several times, but are you AGI-pilled?

Yes. Are you?

No. I read your book, and it’s as close as I’ve ever gotten. That line about next-token prediction just always overcoming its skeptics just really hit me, because it has overcome my skepticism several times now.

But this is why I was asking about talking to a chatbot from three years ago. I feel that wall in the kind of intelligence these things are. Even though I have set off agents to do all kinds of things, there’s a brittleness to it that feels inherent to the technology to me.

Did the Millennium Prize solution change that view at all?

Only in the sense that finding the next thing that has some objective verifiability seems very rich for these tools. So obviously mathematics has a verifiability, and the tools got so capable that they could run at it really, really hard. The brittleness that I’m describing is a lot of the world around us does not have that kind of verifiability.

So I set off Muse to fill out a document on some janky government website, and the website cannot tell Muse what it’s getting right or wrong, and it just collapses. You can blame that on the underlying model not being at the frontier, but there’s just some part of that experience with LLM-based technologies that makes me feel they’re brittle in very specific ways, and they haven’t overcome that sensation for me.

I’m not saying they’re not incredibly capable. I’m not saying that, as enterprise software, they will not automate virtually every business in the world in some way. I’m not saying that my wife isn’t a lawyer who uses Claude every day. It’s all there.

But there’s some part of it where my skepticism is about whether it can overcome its brittleness to become the machine god. I’m excited to see if they can do it, but I don’t see the path from where I sit.

You think there’s sort of a natural plateau at just below human-level intelligence?

I think the human-level intelligence to me, and this is just more philosophical, is defined by novel problem solving — looking at a thing, and understanding that there are multiple paths to a solution, and not having one of those needing to be objectively right to get to the end.

What would it take? What would you have to see to have the scales fall from your eyes and go, “I, Nilay Patel, am fully AGI-pilled”? What would convince you?

I would have to see... You have young children. I have young children. There’s a thing that young children do where they fall down the stairs, and you just see the lights all go on: “I’ve learned this, I will know it forever, and now I’m going to build on that.”

Maybe they’re going to announce recursive self-improvement at the AI labs and that will be the thing that drops the scales from my eyes. But the brittleness that I’m talking about is I see the opposite of that in my children. I’m assuming you see the opposite of it in yours. When they fail, they know about that failure forever. To me, there’s just something very, very core to being human, where every now and again I wake up, and I’m embarrassed about something that happened in high school, and that drives me to do a bunch of stuff, or it drives me to not make a bunch of decisions.

I think that is just a key part of our intelligence. I’m not saying it has to be a key part of every intelligence, but the brittleness I see with the AI systems that I use today is that they’re still computers in a very specific way. They still act like computers. They’re good at solving problems that you can test. They’re good at software engineering. I don’t know that that way of thinking extends into every domain.

I hope you’re right.

That’s my point of view. I call it software brain. You hear the AI CEO say, “We solve coding, and now we can solve everything.” And to me, I’m saying, “That assumes everything happens inside of a computer, and in fact, most things don’t.”

You sure? You sure your brain’s not just a fleshy computer?

I am 100 percent sure of that.

No. I think I’ve read this from you in the past, and I’ve certainly read it from other people, that the machines of our time dominate our own explanations of ourselves. So in the era of the steam engine, our self-conception was that we were steam engines, or in early computers, we were early computers, right? I still call it horsepowering through a problem because I’m a car person.

You don’t think that the AI industry has convinced itself that they are AI because that is the machine of our time?

I don’t know. I’m not a theory of mind guy. I’m not a cognitive neuroscientist. I think that to believe that what’s going on in your head and my head right now is not a form of computation, you have to be kind of a dualist or you have to be kind of a religious person. You have to think there is some spirit, some soul, some secret sauce of cognition that is not just data entering and being processed and transforming inputs into outputs.

Look, I know that is the least romantic, most San Francisco way of explaining what human cognition is. I just have not heard a compelling argument that it is not how our brains work that doesn’t involve some sort of supernatural or immaterial substance.

There’s a surprising number of neuroscientists and religious scholars listening to the show. They’re going to come find you.

They will.

I’m confident. Let me just ask you this. There’s a surprising amount of religiosity in Silicon Valley right now. We just published the Peter Thiel lectures on The Verge. He’s talking about the Antichrist. Do you think these ideas are connected, that we are building God such that they seek God?

Yes. I think we will absolutely have AI religions. I think AI is posing all of the same questions as a religion that we would not otherwise be asking of God. “What is our purpose? What is our meaning? Why are we here?” These are the questions that people now talk about in the context of AI.

I often tell people that being in San Francisco these days feels like living in Europe during the Reformation, where you just have crazy wild-eyed prophets waving their pamphlets around and trying to get you to join their thing. This is what walking down Market Street in San Francisco feels like.

What dropped the scales from your eyes? What made you AGI-pilled?

Bing’s Sydney, believe it or not.

Yeah?

I mean, that was the start. And then from there, it was just kind of a gradual process. One day I realized when I used these things, I wasn’t treating them like an intellectual inferior. I was in some ways treating them as a peer, and that’s when I realized, “Oh, something’s happened here.”

So it’s possible I have AI psychosis. It would not be the first time I’ve heard that, but every time that I have thought, “Okay, it can’t possibly get any better than this, this has to be the plateau,” I’ve been wrong.

So I’m just learning to approach these things with some humility, and maybe the crazy people who have been predicting that scaling would continue indefinitely are right. If they are, I think we need to learn about them, A, and why they think that, and B, try to figure out what to do about it.

Well, Kevin, I’m confident the next time you come on the show, I will have set up a fully AI influencer to make money doing [user-generated content] ads, which is the true future of, I think, all of our businesses.

The podcast is Machine Gods. It’s very good. You host it with Casey Newton. And the book is excellent. It’s The AGI Chronicles. Kevin, thank you so much for being on Decoder.

Thanks. It was great to see you.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

Decoder with Nilay Patel

A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.

title: YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos
snippet: After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all. more…
fullText:
After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all.

Update 10/22: YouTube has confirmed this is not a public-facing test.

YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening

In 2021, YouTube removed the dislike count as a way to “de-weaponize” the button – effort that had been ongoing for years – with YouTube even acknowledging that it was a decision that users might disagree with. Now, following similar changes to Shorts, YouTube appears to be testing further hiding the dislike button.

A report on Twitter/X highlighted by Neowin showcases YouTube hiding the dislike button under an overflow menu, hiding it from view despite the like button remaining front and center. This appears to be on the desktop website, though we couldn’t replicate the same behavior on our end.

	

It’s not the only case of this happening, though.

	

Over the past couple of weeks, reports on Reddit have seen the dislike button vanish, with another web user seeing a slightly different UI to the one above, but with the same result of offloading the button to an overflow menu alongside the “Report” button. 

YouTube runs tests like this frequently, but given the same change was made to the dislike button on Shorts several months ago, it’s all but certain that the same will happen to standard videos.

What do you think of the change?

More on YouTube:

YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium

YouTube begins rolling out GIF support for comments very slowly; it’s for a reason

YouTube bringing automatic background play to Android Automotive cars

Follow Ben: Twitter/X, Threads, Bluesky, and Instagram

title: 7 iPhone Duo Apps That Take Full Advantage of the New Foldable Phone
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo brings iOS to a bigger tablet-like display, and these creative apps are already optimized to make the most of it.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo is easily the most experimental iPhone that Apple has released. That’s both good news and bad news.

On one hand, the shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos.

		

			

On the other hand, the device is so new to iOS that some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s getting an iPhone Duo today (or soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested. 

1. Netflix

Netflix on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent. 

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

2. NYT Cooking

NYT Cooking on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

3. Fantastical

Fantastical on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

4. Edits by Instagram

Edits on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

5 and 6. TikTok and Instagram

Instagram on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

7. Toastie

Toastie on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster. 

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

There are many ways to pair up apps on the iPhone Duo for your convenience.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Bonus: Your duo of choice

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other. 

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

title: Google Health 5.11 rolling out with Fitbit Air Health Guardian, improved sleep tracking, & more
snippet: Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch. more…
fullText:
Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch.

The Improved Automatic Activity Tracking is available now for the Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5, with the Fitbit Edge getting the capabilities at launch on October 27.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to up to 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, we now factor in more context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half.2

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to the Google Health app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

The Fitbit Air and Edge are getting two Health Guardian features if you’re a Google Health Premium subscriber. You can set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends now, with the first report available at the beginning of November.

Blood pressure trends, which allow you to track blood pressure patterns before they can put strain on your heart, will be available in the Health Guardian section of the Health tab if you’ve worn your Fitbit Air for 5 or more consecutive days in October.

Insulin resistance trends, which track monthly shifts in your metabolic health, will be available if you’ve worn your watch for 7 or more days and nights in October.

Blood glucose is now “Glucose” throughout the Google Health app with updated charts and graphs. Additionally:

	

Custom time-in-range goals: You can now set specific time-in-range goals for glucose data from connected continuous glucose monitors. To set a goal, go to the Metabolic section of the Health tab, tap Glucose, open Settings, and select Set goal.

Faster syncing with Lingo by Abbott (US only): You can now connect Lingo by Abbott directly to the Google Health app so your glucose data syncs faster — displaying in the Google Health app within 30 minutes of a reading. If you have a Google Health Premium membership, Google Health Coach³ can also answer questions about your glucose trends. To connect, tap your profile icon in the Google Health app and select Partner Apps.³

Finally, there’s improved Sleep Tracking across wake detection and nap editing:

More accurate awake detection: We’ve improved our sleep tracking to better factor in your steps data so that we can more accurately track short awakenings, like getting up to use the bathroom. 

Easier nap editing: You’re always in control of your sleep data. If a nap ever shows up that doesn’t match your day, you can now easily remove it directly from your nap card.

Version 5.11 is available on iOS and still rolling out for Android users.

title: The iPhone Duo Hit Stores Friday. Next Came Long Lines, Sellouts and Resellers
snippet: Crowds camped outside of stores before Apple’s first folding phone became available.
fullText:
Apple’s causing a commotion with its new iPhone Duo. 

The tech giant’s first foldable phone hit shelves Friday, and lines were forming (and selling out) well before Apple stores even opened. Many preordered the phone, but that didn’t stop people from trying their luck to buy one without an order number. CNET editors and reporters were on the ground to bring you all of the uproar, so you can save yourself the trip if you were trying to buy one over the weekend.

At Apple’s flagship 5th Avenue location in New York, the line started forming on Wednesday by 9 a.m. ET — two days before the launch. Over 50 people were waiting in line by Thursday at 7 p.m. ET, sometimes with buckets serving as placeholders. In the first minutes after the store opened, there was no word that the iPhone Duo had sold out yet, but other stores were sold out before their doors opened.

The Oxmoor Center opened at 6 a.m. ET for Apple fans planning to buy the iPhone Duo on launch day. Faith Chihil/CNET

At the Oxmoor Center in Louisville, Kentucky, the Apple store opened at 8 a.m. EDT, and CNET’s Faith Chihil saw a line of more than 40 people three hours earlier. At about 7:27 a.m. ET, Apple store employees started taking orders for the phone. But the 256GB iPhone Duo was already sold out.

		

			

Lines gather outside of Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, where the iPhone Duo sold out before 7:30 a.m. ET.David Katzmaier / CNET

CNET Editor in Chief David Katzmaier reported that the first person was in line at Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET, and was able to preorder the phone. Apple store employees started taking orders to pick up the phone at 7 a.m. ET.  But by 7:30 a.m. ET, the rest of the line was dismissed after an announcement that the store had sold out before doors opened.

CNET’s Patrick Holland reported from Apple’s Union Square store in San Francisco. The first people started forming a line at 9:30 p.m. ET on Thursday. As of 11 a.m. ET, lines were down the block and around the building. There were also some sightings of people reselling the iPhone Duo just moments after waiting in line to buy one.

The line for the iPhone Duo started at 9:30 p.m. ET on Thursday at Apple’s Union Square store in San Francisco.Patrick Holland / CNET

Meanwhile, at the Apple store at University Village in Seattle, about 180 people were waiting in line who didn’t preorder the iPhone Duo. It sold out within 15 minutes of the store opening.

While many may have expected new Apple CEO John Ternus to be at the New York flagship store, he debuted the iPhone Duo launch at the Apple store in Austin, Texas. He might have been there because of this weekend’s Formula 1 race in the city — streaming on Apple TV.

iPhone Duo buyers had ‘one more thing’ waiting at pickup

Apple is full of surprises. In line with the company’s “one more thing” tagline, those who preordered the iPhone Duo had a surprise awaiting them at unboxing.

Apple’s usual “Hello” welcome screen included their name when they first turned on the phone. It’s clearly a special detail the company thought of before today, and it’s the first time it has customized its usual welcome screen for customers.

Jean Vasquez, founder of True Skies, shows off his iPhone Duo with his name on the opening screen. Bridget Carey / CNET

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s long-awaited first foldable iPhone, debuted earlier this month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It features split-screen capabilities, a photo preview display, Touch ID instead of Face ID and Apple Pencil support. The iPhone Duo’s preorders opened on Oct. 16, but quickly turned into a backlog that stretches into early next year. Pricing starts at $1,999.

“Details like the matte inner display, under-display inner camera and smooth transitions between screens give the Duo a premium feel that helps to justify its high price tag, at least to some extent,” CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti said in her review of the iPhone Duo.

The Duo, Al-Heeti said, “is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general. But I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.”

We don’t know how many iPhone Duos are available at each store or when Apple will restock its physical locations. But there’s a limit of two iPhone Duos per person, per day, which marks the first time in a long time that Apple’s put a cap on how many you can buy. 

If you’re set on getting the phone, try ordering on Apple’s website and picking it up at a nearby store to get the phone sooner, but you’ll need to check availability on Oct. 24. It could be sooner than its estimated shipping times that say the phone won’t arrive until Jan. 29 in some areas.

title: I’ve struggled to use Samsung displays for years, but the Galaxy S27 may finally fix that; here’s why
snippet: The Samsung Galaxy S27 display may be getting a DC-dimming upgrade, and that will be a huge boon for people sensitive to PWM dimming. more…
fullText:
The Samsung Galaxy S27 display may be getting a DC-dimming upgrade, and that will be a huge boon for people sensitive to PWM dimming.

Ever since the Galaxy Z Fold 4, I’ve had difficulty using Samsung phones for long periods of time. The problem, for me, is the company’s use of low-frequency PWM dimming, which causes me horrid headaches, followed by eye pain, and eventually nausea. It’s not fun, and I’ve learned through resources like r/PWM_Sensitive and LEDStrain.org that I’m not alone.

Thankfully, Samsung’s Galaxy S27‘s display may give users the option to use DC dimming, according to one rumor (via GSMArena). Motorola has offered DC dimming as an option on all its OLED-equipped phones for years, and it’ll be great to see Samsung do the same. DC dimming is a more traditional dimming method used by lightbulbs and displays since the dawn of each technology, and is often considered more comfortable than PWM dimming by advocacy groups.

Sure enough, as I learned more about PWM dimming in my personal struggle over the years, phones that use DC dimming are often the most comfortable for me. The only other alternative is to use much higher frequency PWM dimming; 2,000Hz or higher, while the $1,300 Galaxy S26 Ultra only uses 480Hz.

	

Samsung has long prioritized PWM dimming on its displays for several reasons. First, PWM dimming offers better display quality in low-light situations, as DC-dimmed OLEDs can sometimes exhibit “mura” at low brightness levels, which means individual pixels don’t dim at the same rate. This creates what’s referred to as a “noisy” display, and often looks a bit like old film cameras (see the image below for an example).

Second, is efficiency. While it hasn’t been proven to have a drastic effect, PWM dimming can be loosely linked to better battery life. This has become a bigger deal in recent years as Samsung has lagged behind other companies in battery technology, but will be less of a sticking point as the company finally adopts silicon-carbon batteries more widely.

Third, is cost. DC dimming traditionally requires extra hardware to regulate voltage, while PWM dimming is (typically) done entirely via software. Extra hardware means a phone costs more to manufacture, even if it’s just a small amount per unit.

But people who are sensitive to PWM dimming typically cannot use Samsung phones at all, so none of these “positive” points matter to them. Companies like Apple and Google have begun making changes to cater toward PWM-sensitive individuals, but neither have adopted full DC dimming as this Galaxy S27 display rumor suggests Samsung might do.

If the Galaxy S27 display doesn’t adopt DC dimming next year, that will make the Motorola Signature 27 the only flagship in the US to support the technology. OnePlus used to offer DC dimming on its flagship phones in the US, but the company no longer sells its phones outside of China.

title: iFixit’s look inside the iPhone Duo may explain those broken screens and hinges
snippet: As is tradition, iFixit has torn open the latest iPhone and laid its parts bare on a table. fullText:
Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

As is tradition, iFixit has torn open the latest iPhone and laid its parts bare on a table. It found some interesting details about how Apple might be hiding the crease on the Duo’s folding screen and gave it a 5/10 repairability score. That might not seem particularly high, but it’s the best score the site has given to a foldable yet.

The internal screen’s matte nano-texture cover doesn’t just make it more readable in bright sunlight; it also helps mask the crease by scattering reflections. When looking at the display under a microscope, iFixit also found oval-shaped subpixels arranged at various angles, which the site believes are designed to reduce artifacts and further mask the crease down the middle of the display.

The nano-texture outer layer is relatively easy to replace without swapping out the OLED underneath. If you do need to repair the display itself, however, good luck. As is the case with other foldables, it’s an expensive nightmare. Dust did make it into the USB-C port, speaker grills, and the hinge — making it a bit crunchy. But noticeably less of the glow dust found its way inside the phone than the Z Fold8 or Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

As for reports of damaged screens and cracking hinges, iFixit has some theories. The hinge on the iPhone Duo is incredibly complex, and they suspect part of it sometimes isn’t descending properly. There is also an accordion cable that passes over that exact spot, and it’s near the edge of the battery. It’s possible this is concentrating pressure and leading to the “audible crack” reported by some and the broken screens. Apple did not immediately return a request for comment.

fullText:
In my mind, Spooky Season music comes in two distinct flavors. There are the fun, occasionally goofy songs like “The Monster Mash” and John Carpenter’s “Halloween Theme.” Then there is the genuinely terrifying: Throbbing Gristle, The Body, or Scott Walker’s The Drift.

This 2006 album from the singer-songwriter is truly upsetting. On it, Walker explores death, disease, and tragedy. But not just from some abstract perspective. There are visceral descriptions of the hanging of Benito Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci. He sings about 9/11, his stillborn twin brother, and the Srebrenica genocide. Lyrically, it’s about as dark as an album gets.

But it’s the experimental backdrop that drives it all home.

At times, the record sounds more like the score to an Ari Aster film than anything that could be called pop music under even the most generous definitions. Seasick guitars in the verses of “Jesse” give way to dissonant strings that drone oppressively over the chorus. You can feel the low-bitrate MP3 noise that opens “Clara” in your jaw, which also allegedly features the sound of his percussionist punching a pig carcass as part of the rhythm track.

Songs stop on a dime, linger in uncomfortable silence, then erupt in bursts of mechanical noise. Animal bleating, foley work, and atonal orchestra sections grind against Walker’s warble. Nothing is ever quite in tune, and it can be challenging to get through the record in a single sitting if you’re not in a very particular mood. But sticking with it can be quite rewarding.

Some songs and performances are so beautiful they send shivers down your spine or give you goosebumps. Scott Walker’s The Drift is the opposite of that. You will still have an involuntary physical reaction, but it’s more shudders than shivers. It will make your skin crawl.

Scott Walker’s The Drift is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including YouTube Music, Apple Music, Qobuz, Deezer, and Spotify.

Terrence O'Brien
excerpt:
In my mind, Spooky Season music comes in two distinct flavors. There are the fun, occasionally goofy songs like “The Monster Mash” and John Carpenter’s “Halloween Theme.” Then there is the genuinely terrifying: Throbbing Gristle, The Body, or Scott Walker’s The Drift.

This 2006 album from the singer-songwriter is truly upsetting. On it, Walker explores death, disease, and tragedy. But not just from some abstract perspective. There are visceral descriptions of the hanging of Benito Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci. He sings about 9/11, his stillborn twin brother, and the Srebrenica genocide. Lyrically, it’s about as dark as an album gets.

Today is the 25th anniversary of Apple unveiling the first iPod. And as discovered by Kian on X, the company’s website now has a fun new iPod easter egg.

Apple marks 25th anniversary of iPod introduction with new easter egg

The iPod is 25 years old and has long been discontinued, but it lives on in the hearts of many fans.

And now, a digital version lives on as an easter egg on Apple’s website too.

If you visit music.apple.com and add a path that doesn’t exist, the ‘Page Not Found’ screen now features a fully interactive original iPod model.

You can try it out by visiting music.apple.com/ipod or any other nonexistent version of the domain.

The iPod on the page lets you click through using its buttons to find pre-installed songs. The scroll wheel even works by clicking and dragging it around.

Apple first introduced the iPod on October 23, 2001, and the music you’ll find on this interactive model comes from artists that were popular at the time.

	

You can select songs to play 90-second previews right there in the web interface.

It’s a fun easter egg to play around with and celebrate the iPod’s legacy.

title: Apple TV’s long-awaited Fleetwood Mac documentary finally has a release date
snippet: Nearly two years after it was first announced, Fleetwood Mac fans won’t have to wait much longer for Frank Marshall’s documentary about the legendary band to arrive on Apple TV. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Nearly two years after it was first announced, Fleetwood Mac fans won’t have to wait much longer for Frank Marshall’s documentary about the legendary band to arrive on Apple TV. Here are the details.

’First-ever fully authorized Fleetwood Mac documentary’

Apple TV today confirmed the premiere date and title of its upcoming Fleetwood Mac documentary film, directed by Frank Marshall (The Beach Boys, From Earth to the Moon).

As the platform confirmed earlier today in a post on X, “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” is set to premiere on Friday, January 29, 2027.

Apple TV says “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” offers fans “a definitive and unprecedented look at Fleetwood Mac’s story, bringing together the voices, memories and perspectives of Grammy Award-winning Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks.”

“Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” will join Apple TV’s growing catalog of music documentaries, which already includes “Beastie Boys Story,” “The Velvet Underground,” “Billie Eilish: The World’s a Little Blurry,” “Louis Armstrong’s Black & Blues,” and “Bono: Stories of Surrender,” among others.

Here’s a little more more of what Apple TV had to say about “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain”:

Following their fortuitous meeting in 1974, Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks reflect on their uncompromising 50-plus-year history, from their record-breaking recordings and tours — including never-before-seen footage and exclusive new interviews — through to today. The film explores how the band’s trials and tribulations, personal resilience and musical dexterity combined to create songs that have stood the test of time and are enduring masterpieces. It takes fans through the highs and lows of their brilliant career, illuminating the exceptional ingredients each member brought to the band’s uncommon alchemy — a musical union that sold more than 220 million records worldwide. The documentary explores what allowed this combination of artists to create singular musical work again and again, and what drew them back together and held them there when every possible pressure, both outside and inside the band, threatened to blow them apart.

While there’s no full trailer for “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” just yet, Apple TV has shared a short teaser on X, which you can watch below:

title: iPhone Duo reviews: The absolute best foldable phone, but not without compromise
snippet: We posted our own review of the iPhone Duo yesterday, and Chance Miller was left convinced that “this form factor represents the future of the iPhone,” while acknowledging that the first-gen iPhone Duo comes with trade-offs. I think what surprised me most is the degree of consensus found across the reviews, given the generally polarized appeal of foldable phones. That’s not to say reviewers think everyone should buy one, but there is widespread agreement on the pros and cons – starting with five key takeouts … more…
fullText:
We posted our own review of the iPhone Duo yesterday, and Chance Miller was left convinced that “this form factor represents the future of the iPhone,” while acknowledging that the first-gen iPhone Duo comes with trade-offs.

I think what surprised me most is the degree of consensus found across the reviews, given the generally polarized appeal of foldable phones. That’s not to say reviewers think everyone should buy one, but there is widespread agreement on the pros and cons – starting with five key takeouts …

Five key takeouts

First, all the reviews I’ve read and watched say that the iPhone Duo is hands-down the best foldable phone on the market. Apple waited a very long time before joining the foldable party, and it seems clear that it was absolutely right to do so.

Second, this phone is absolutely not for everyone. Even leaving aside the high purchase cost, the form factor currently involves compromises that would rule it out for some.  If you expect to use the outer screen most of the time and only unfold it a few times a day, then the trade-offs of the heavy weight when held in one hand and the unusual display shape are just too big a drawback. This phone really only makes sense if you expect to make frequent use of the larger unfolded screen in your day-to-day use.

Third, Apple hasn’t made the crease invisible, and indeed has made no claims to do so. You can see it in certain lights at certain angles, and you can feel it when running your finger across the screen. But everyone agrees that this is the least intrusive crease ever seen on a foldable, and that it’s simply not an issue in real life use. More on this in a moment.

Fourth, a great many apps haven’t yet been updated, and in the worst case that means seeing an iPhone screen layout stranded in the middle of a mostly black inner display. The optimistic view is that this will rapidly change, but be prepared for some disappointments with third-party apps in early usage.

Finally, going back to Touch ID is a significant compromise after being used to Face ID. We do have to bear in mind that reviewers have only had a chance to use the device for a week, but certainly in that time most say they didn’t really get used to it and would absolutely prefer Face ID.

Fold testing

A couple of reviewers used machines to subject the iPhone Duo to thousands of folds and unfolds to test two things. Does the crease become significantly more visible over time, and how does the hinge hold up? 

In both cases, there is a measurable impact. Joanna Stern’s tests found that the hinge is affected across tens of thousands of folds, but interestingly becomes stiffer rather than looser – the opposite of what we would expect. However, while this change was measurable using a strain gauge after 32,000 folds, she said she couldn’t feel it in normal use.

HTX Studio did the most scientific testing of the impact of thousands of folds on the crease. The depth of the crease when new was measured at just 48 microns, about half the thickness of a sheet of paper, while the slope of the crease measured at less than 0.1 degrees – both markedly better than competing foldables. After 3,000 folds, the depth of the crease increased to 167 microns and the slope increased to 1.24 degrees. That brings it more in line with the measurements of other foldables after the same number of tests.

The bottom line

There are links to the full reviews, but here is the bottom line from each …

Joanna Stern:

After 20 years of iPhones that look mostly the same, it’s exciting to see Apple chart a new course. But the Duo is still one of the most early adopter Apple products I’ve tested in a long time. It’s easy to imagine what Gen 2 will look like. It’s lighter, there’s Face ID, a better camera inside, and hopefully a lower price. Also, it’s got a telephoto camera, and it’s no longer a hand warmer. 

The good news is most of my other frustrations can be fixed with software updates and developers figuring out how to make great apps for two very different screen sizes. Sure, early adopters have to navigate some choppy waters, but as Apple developers catch up, I can see smoother sailing ahead.

HTX Studio:

Apple’s first attempt [at a foldable] brings plenty of fresh ideas with real purpose behind them that deserves credit. But think about it: these ideas mostly fix flaws built into the folding design rather than pushing the phone experience forward. 

[Will this make foldables mainstream?] I still doubt it because this design has two fundamental conflicts at its core. First, the [aspect ratios] of two screens work against each other. Improve the outer screen and the inner screen becomes a big empty square. Favor the inner screen [as Apple has done] and the outer screen becomes a passport that’s hard to grip. It’s a zero-sum game. More importantly, whatever the balance, you get a makeshift phone outside and a cut down tablet inside. Neither delivers the best

experience.

Second, the benefits are occasional, but the cost are constant. To fit a hinge and the big screen, it sacrifices weight, battery life, cooling, performance, cameras, and most importantly, price. But use one or watch other people do and you’ll see they mostly use the outer screen […] You enjoy the benefits some of the time but pay the price all the time.

Daring Fireball:

If you really want to do something, or sit back and read or watch something, the big display is fantastic. But that Duo-as-tablet experience is so cumbersome compared to the “just look at it” experience of using a regular iPhone uno that you simply cannot do it every time you use the Duo. You will use the outer display quite a bit. And using the outer display delivers the worst iPhone experience ever. I mean, some iPhone has to be the one that offered the worst iPhone experience ever. That iPhone is the outer half of the iPhone Duo […]

If you’d rather trade your iPhone for an iPad Mini that you can fold in half to carry around, the iPhone Duo might be the form factor for you. Even if that’s the case, though, this first iPhone Duo might not suit you, for all the various irritations and shortcomings I’ve documented […] It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry.

CNET:

Aside from some minor shortcomings, Apple appears to have stuck the landing with its long-awaited foldable. Hopefully, future iterations will add elements such as Face ID while improving the camera capabilities, either by adding a telephoto lens or bolstering the inner screen’s FaceTime camera. It would be nice to see multitasking become more dynamic in the future, too.

[But] most people just don’t need a phone that doubles as a tablet. [While the Duo] is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general, I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.

Gizmodo:

Whether you’re an iPhone fan, foldable evangelist, or Android user who’s just been waiting to see what Apple offers, I think we can all agree that the iPhone Duo has already achieved what competing foldables have not been able to in seven years: generate considerable buzz for foldable phones […] This is what we’ve been waiting for after more than a decade of matured bar-style phones. Finally, phone hardware and software are genuinely exciting again, which is something to celebrate […]

As for whether you should get the iPhone Duo—that depends on if you can afford it, either buying it outright, paying in installments, or leasing it through the Apple Upgrade program. Do you want a foldable phone, and why? Will you use the larger screen often, and how much value will you get from it? Will the weight bother you? Do you need better cameras? There are so many personal factors to consider before you decide. The iPhone Duo isn’t the “definitive” iPhone to own. Apple’s iPhone lineup now caters to every budget and every type of user. Only you can be honest with yourself about your needs.

	

Tom’s Guide:

The iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable phone I’ve ever tested, with a sturdy and premium build and a nano-texture display that hides the crease. I also like the multiple usage modes and split-screen multitasking. However, while fully updated apps for the Duo look great, non-optimized apps do not. And the lack of a telephoto zoom is a bummer for a $2,000 phone […]

I like the iPhone Duo’s nano texture display in that it greatly reduces glare outdoors and minimizes the crease better than any foldable I’ve tested. But you give up perfect blacks with this matte panel and more saturated colors versus the iPhone 18 Pro Max. You also sacrifice a telephoto lens and Face ID. I can live with those trade-offs, but that doesn’t mean I like them.

In a way it’s a good thing that the iPhone Duo is backordered for many until December or January. That will give developers plenty of time to update their offerings for this foldable. I don’t think it will take that long, though, based on the high demand.

Overall, though, I think the iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable yet with the most polished, intuitive and fun software experience.

Wired:

This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues but because I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.

Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but, on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).

But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.

The Verge:

There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way. It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief […] But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going […]

We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time […] Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera […]

But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time […] The real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.

What’s your take after reading the review conclusions? Have the reviews made you more or less interested in the iPhone Duo? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
