title: Apple’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ highlights creative projects from emerging designers
snippet: Apple, in collaboration with Design Miami, is highlighting four creative projects from emerging designers in this year’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple, in collaboration with Design Miami, is highlighting four creative projects from emerging designers in this year’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris. Here are the details.

Apple showcases 2026 Designers of Tomorrow

Apple today published an interesting press release highlighting the work of five designers, who “integrated Apple products into their creative processes” to develop their projects.

Now in its second year, Apple’s “Designers of Tomorrow” initiative is organized in partnership with Design Miami. As Apple explains, this year’s participants were selected by a jury that included the company’s vice president of industrial design, Molly Anderson.

Here’s Apple on this year’s theme and the designers’ approach to it:

“Apple’s Designers of Tomorrow showcase, in collaboration with Design Miami, returns for a second year to spotlight the best in emerging talent, this time focusing on the theme of presence. Exploring what still holds the public’s attention amid the hurried pace of the modern world, designers Salem S. Charabi, Isabel Rower, Yoonjeong Lee, and Parafernalia (Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla) crafted original works that invite reflection and aim to shift perspectives, engage the senses, and kindle curiosity.”

According to Rodman Primack, the program’s curator, the artists’ works “demonstrate the power of objects to shape our physical environments and transform the human experiences that are possible within them.”

Throughout the press release, Apple details how the selected designers used its products to develop their projects. Egyptian-Danish architect Charabi, for instance, relied on a MacBook Pro for sketching and 3D modeling, while Seoul-based designer Lee used an iPad Pro and Apple Pencil to sketch ideas and take notes.

Lee’s New Form sketches (left) and Parafernalia’s MonoAmbiente 1 sketch (right)

Brooklyn-based designer Rower says she used an iPhone to document her creative process and Keynote to experiment with images and text, while the duo behind Mexican design studio Parafernalia said they used the iPhone, iPad Pro, and Procreate to collaborate remotely between Monterrey and Mexico City via FaceTime.

As with Apple’s recent showcase of the “From Earth to Sky” fashion collection, it may be tempting to dismiss the exhibition as a marketing effort. But if you’re into design, it’s always interesting to see how professional designers use the same tools we’re familiar with to come up with such different kinds of creative work.

Update, 4:56 p.m. ET: Apple’s Greg Joswiak shared a post on X featuring a video highlighting the designers’ work:

Different paths. Different crafts. One shared spark.

Check out four emerging designers at Design Miami Paris, each bringing their vision to life with iPhone, iPad Pro, Apple Pencil Pro, and MacBook Pro. pic.twitter.com/pZfMV1Gsf8

title: John Ternus talks his involvement with design teams at Apple
snippet: Last week TIME shared select quotes from a new interview with Apple CEO John Ternus, but today the full video has been published, including a discussion on Ternus’s involvement with Apple’s design teams. more…
fullText:
Last week TIME shared select quotes from a new interview with Apple CEO John Ternus, but today the full video has been published, including a discussion on Ternus’s involvement with Apple’s design teams.

John Ternus says that at Apple ‘design means everything to us’

Ever since John Ternus officially became CEO last month, reporting has indicated that he’s spending lots of his time hands-on with Apple’s design teams.

In a recent interview with TIME, Ternus discusses his new role, the transition, and his current priorities. And design comes up in the conversation.

At one point he’s asked directly: “How involved with design are you still?”

Here’s what Ternus said:

It’s funny because as a product designer—I’m a mechanical engineer by background—the team that the product designers work most closely with are the industrial designers. So, I’ve been working hand in hand with industrial designers at Apple since I started. And it’s an amazing relationship. 

I think what’s so special about this place is design is at the center of it. Design means everything to us. And what’s incredible is our designers, both on the software side and the hardware side, they really understand the engineering. And the engineers have a very deep appreciation for design. And so it’s a really powerful collaboration. It’s not [like] a designer sketches something up and then throws it over the wall and says, “Go make that.” From the very beginning the teams are collaborating, and it’s just a wonderful thing to be a part of.

Without explicitly saying that he’s been especially hands-on with the design teams, Ternus emphasizes that he’s always worked closely with Apple designers, and reiterates how central design is to the company.

title: This clever USB-C cable doubles as a stand for your phone [Gallery]
snippet: One of my favorite things about the rise of magnetic wireless charging has been the prevalence of chargers that hold my phone upright on my nightstand. But, when travelling, that tends to be a bit more cumbersome, or at least a little more expensive. The folks over at Statik have come up with a clever solution, a USB-C cable that has a kickstand for your phone with no added bulk. more…
fullText:
One of my favorite things about the rise of magnetic wireless charging has been the prevalence of chargers that hold my phone upright on my nightstand. But, when travelling, that tends to be a bit more cumbersome, or at least a little more expensive. The folks over at Statik have come up with a clever solution, a USB-C cable that has a kickstand for your phone with no added bulk.

The Statik PowerStand is a pretty straightforward idea. A USB-C cable that has a kickstand at the end. Simple idea, plenty of room for a poor implementation, but this is really quite well done.

One end of the braided cable is a standard USB-C plug, while the other side has a right-angle plug on an extended base. Admittedly, it feels a little clunky on its own, but it makes sense once you plug in a device. The USB-C plug is angled slightly and on a raised base, easily connecting to your phone even if it’s in a case. Two foldable “feet” swivel out and let you either stand the phone up vertically – perfect for charging – or put it horizontally for something like watching a video.

The implementation here is really quite good. The vertical orientation is surprisingly well-balanced and I never felt like my phone would just fall over. Don’t get me wrong, a shove will definitely let it fall over, but it’s not just going to fall on its own. The spacing for cases also worked perfectly on a Nomad case I have for my iPhone or my wife’s Peak Design Pixel 10 Pro case, but the plug didn’t feel insecure on my case-less Pixel as a result. 

	

The foldable “feet” also slot into place quickly and lock into position pretty well. It’s a good balance between strength and easily being able to adjust the position.

This isn’t some shoddy cable either. It’s a 240W cable with USB 2.0 data transfer speeds and is measures 6.6ft long too. The braided texture feels sturdy and it’s nice that the design still lets you use the kickstand end with a laptop. 

	

The Statik PowerStand easily earned a permanent spot in my travel bag, and for $20, it’s definitely worth your consideration too. 

Statik, by the way, is the same brand that makes those magnetic cables that are easier to store because they attach to themselves. Another cable in its lineup that the company sent out with the PowerStand is the PowerPivot Pro, an all-in-one cable with USB-C and USB-A ends on one side with a USB-C tip on the other end that can rotate in any direction. I’m not quite as keen on the functionality there, but Statik points out the one place it might come in handy – the car. For Android Auto/CarPlay, I could see this one being good for having your phone perhaps stuffed into a tight spot. It’d been even better, though, if both ends of the cable had these rotating tips. If nothing else, Statik says this is 20x tougher than a normal cable, and I believe it after feeling it in person.

title: Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji
snippet: Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices.

One Pixel 6a user on Reddit shared his new 3D emoji library, noting that his choices switched over from the traditional designs. Given that this is on a Pixel 6a, it signals Google might be slowly switching devices over from 2D to 3D emojis. Only one other commenter shared the same experience, which means the rollout, if it’s actually going live, is very gradual.

Without many other reports, it’s hard to nail down Google’s intended device targets. We know the Pixel 11 is how Google wanted to release the new 3D emoji set, but what comes after has seemed slow. So far, it looks like a majority of devices represented in that thread haven’t received an update. The one user who said they got the new Noto 3D emoji set said they appeared after a Google Play Store update.

Like them or hate them, Google is replacing the standard cartoonish emoji library with 3D designs that closely emulate them on all Pixel devices going forward, starting with Android 17. There are subtle differences across Android’s emoji selection, and they’ll likely take some time getting used to if you’ve been using Android devices for some time.

title: Slow Horses showrunner explains finale shock ending, season 7 trailer debuts
snippet: The Slow Horses season 6 finale is available now, with a shocking ending that is explained by new showrunner Gaby Chiappe in an interview. Plus, Apple has debuted the first trailer for season 7. more…
fullText:
The Slow Horses season 6 finale is available now, with a shocking ending that is explained by new showrunner Gaby Chiappe in an interview. Plus, Apple has debuted the first trailer for season 7.

Here’s what happened in that surprise Slow Horses finale ending, plus the new trailer for season 7

If you haven’t yet watched the Slow Horses season 6 finale, stop reading here.

**major spoilers ahead**

Slow Horses was marked this season by a high number of character deaths.

That continued in the finale that just aired with the death of Emma Flyte at the hands of River’s father, Frank Harkness.

But in the final moments of the episode, there’s another character who seemingly dies too, and in far more shocking fashion: River Cartwright.

It’s not entirely clear what caused the death, though. Here’s the official explanation from head writer and season 6 showrunner Gaby Chiappe (via Gold Derby):

Actually, the groundwork is laid in Episode 2 when Jim and Jane [the assassins played by Kyle Soller and MyAnna Buring] come knocking on the door and River and Sid are hiding. You see Jim looking around and there’s a little bottle lying on the table. He looks around and sees the crowbar that River brought in with him, and we have to assume that he paints it with what’s in the bottle, which — given that there have been nerve agent attacks elsewhere — it’s a Novichok attack.

We had a lot of debate about that. Will people know what it is and what’s happening? It’s taken from the book, but in the book it’s left on a doorknob, which is slightly different. It’s still the idea that something happened in the corner of your eye, but you didn’t quite know what it was. And the assassin who laid it is long dead now.

Though Chiappe doesn’t technically confirm that River is dead, the season 7 trailer certainly suggests that’s what has happened.

	

Here’s the season 7 trailer that airs at the end of the finale, courtesy of Apple TV News Hub on X:

Apple recently announced that Slow Horses has been renewed through season 8. Season 7 has already completed filming, with an air date expected in or around September 2027.

fullText:
The iPhone Duo is the biggest change to the iPhone’s form factor in its nearly 20-year history. It combines a compact, notebook-style design with an iPad-like inner display. It might look a little awkward, but that’s for good reason. 

I’ve spent the last week using the iPhone Duo. Here’s everything you need to know about Apple’s first foldable iPhone.

Design

In my iPhone 18 Pro review last month, I wrote that the iPhone 18 Pro Max was right at the edge of what I was willing to carry in terms of weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 254 grams, five grams more than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

But one key difference is weight distribution. Despite being slightly heavier, I find the iPhone Duo significantly more comfortable to hold than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The iPhone Duo is shorter and squatter, which makes a big difference in how it feels in my hand.

That said, the iPhone Duo is heavy, and I start to feel it in my wrist when using it one-handed for extended periods. Still, I find it more manageable than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The other aspect of the iPhone Duo’s size is thickness. When closed, the iPhone Duo measures 11.3mm thick, making it about 29% thicker than the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Unfold it, however, and it’s just 5.2mm thick. That’s even thinner than the iPhone Air, which measures 5.64mm.

Then, we have the overall footprint — which I think is particularly notable for the pocketability conversation. When folded, the iPhone Duo measures 117.8mm tall and 84.1mm wide. That makes it 45.6mm shorter than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but just 6.1mm wider.

Despite its added thickness and weight, I’ve found the iPhone Duo surprisingly comfortable to carry in my pockets. Its shorter, wider footprint makes a bigger difference than I expected.

And then, of course, you can take the iPhone Duo out of your pocket and unfold it to reveal that massive 7.6-inch display. That extra weight and thickness is well worth the trade-off.

The iPhone Duo’s hinge is what makes that folding and unfolding possible. Apple says the hinge is made up of more than 100 individual components, with a variable torque system that adjusts resistance as you open and close the device. There’s an integrated magnet system that keeps the two sides securely closed.

Unfolding the iPhone Duo is very much a two-handed operation. The hinge has enough resistance, and the two halves fit together securely enough that you really need both hands to open it comfortably.

When I first unboxed the iPhone Duo, I instinctively wanted to baby it. I was worried about breaking something. It’s a weird sensation to repeatedly fold and unfold an iPhone. That’s not because it didn’t feel durable; it just goes against nearly 20 years of how we’ve used an iPhone.

But after a day or so, I just … stopped thinking about the hinge — and I mean that as a compliment. I’m already treating it like any other iPhone.

The hinge can also hold the iPhone Duo steady at various angles, enabling “seated” and “tent” configurations. This lets you prop up the iPhone Duo on a table to watch videos, take FaceTime calls, or use StandBy, without needing a separate stand or accessory. iPhone Duo features a completely revamped StandBy experience that works without being plugged in. I’ve loved propping it up alongside my MacBook at the coffee shop. 

Apple uses Grade 5 titanium for the iPhone Duo’s frame, with a polished, mirror-like finish. The iPhone Duo is available in Night Sky and Star White. My review unit is Night Sky, a dark blue Apple probably would’ve called midnight a few years ago. It’s nothing particularly exciting, but it shifts between dark blue and black in different lighting.

The iPhone Duo is also IP68-rated for dust and water resistance, like every other iPhone Apple sells today. I didn’t test this, but I’ll take Apple’s word.

All of this comes together to make the iPhone Duo the most versatile iPhone that Apple sells, without compromising durability. On paper, some aspects of the iPhone Duo’s design sound unappealing — it’s thicker and heavier than I’d normally accept from an iPhone.

But it’s hard to overstate just how impressive the whole thing feels in practice. The hinge feels fantastic, the smaller footprint makes it surprisingly easy to carry, and you can unfold it into a 7.6-inch display. It’s an incredible piece of engineering, and even after a week, I’m still impressed by how well the entire package comes together.

Outer display

The iPhone Duo’s outer display measures 5.4 inches diagonally with the same 1.4:1 aspect ratio as the inner display.

On paper, that 5.4-inch outer display sounds small. I’ve seen a lot of people compare it to the iPhone 12/13 mini, which had a 5.4-inch display. It’s a fair comparison on paper, but it doesn’t translate to the real world because of the different aspect ratio.

Thanks to its aspect ratio, Apple says the Duo’s outer display has 90% of the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro.

The iPhone Duo’s squatter, wider form factor feels very different from any other iPhone. The wider proportions give you more horizontal space to work with, but significantly less vertical space than a traditional iPhone (including the aforementioned iPhone mini). Grab your passport and imagine it runs iOS. That’s the best way to describe the form factor.

For a right-handed person, the iPhone Duo is a delight to use one-handed. I can comfortably reach all corners and edges, unlike my iPhone 18 Pro, where I have to stretch to reach the top-left corner.

Typing on the iPhone Duo’s outer screen is very pleasant. Given its shorter design, the keyboard does take up just a little under half of the total screen area. I’ve found both two-handed and one-handed swipe typing to be comfortable.

But while I’m right-handed, I’ve made a point of using my iPhone Duo in my left hand as much as possible, since I’ve seen a lot of left-handed people worried about the right-aligned software controls on iPhone Duo. It’s definitely not as comfortable as using it with my right hand. You’ll struggle to reach the top-right corner to pull down Control Center, but the controls lower down on the right side are still mostly reachable.

The iPhone Duo’s outer display has been great for quick interactions like responding to texts and emails, checking items off a shopping list, and jotting down thoughts in the Notes app. It literally feels like I’m pulling a small, physical notebook out of my pocket.

The outer display has also been excellent for other things, like extended social media scrolling and reading. Those things are undeniably better on the larger inner display (obviously), but if you can’t or don’t want to unfold the iPhone Duo, I don’t feel constrained by the outer display.

But the awkwardness of the iPhone’s 5.4-inch outer display shows up in Safari. The web simply isn’t optimized for this form factor. I’ll talk more about this later, but the right-aligned controls on iPhone Duo eat into the usable screen real estate in Safari especially.

It’s easy to find yourself on a Safari webpage where you can’t see anything but a cookie popup or newsletter banner. Granted, you can’t really blame Apple for that. It’s clear the modern web isn’t optimized for such a small, squat form factor. Once you get to a long-form article, reading in Safari on the outer display is pleasant. Getting there can be a bit annoying, depending on the website design.

I can see why Apple chose the design it did for Safari on the iPhone Duo. I don’t think overlapping the controls with the website would’ve made sense. Still, scrolling in Safari is one of the best examples of something that’s better on the inner screen. 

Ultimately, one thing I was worried about going into my time with the iPhone Duo was that using the outer display would feel like a “last resort.” I worried I’d only want to use it if I was in a situation where unfolding to the larger inner screen wasn’t an option. This hasn’t been the case.

Inner display

Minimizing the crease

There are two aspects to Apple’s work on the iPhone Duo’s crease. First, there’s minimizing the crease itself.

The iPhone Duo’s 7.6-inch inner display is a classic example of Apple’s engineering work at its best. It’s made of more than 10 ultra-thin layers, each designed to balance durability and flexibility for folding.

At the surface, there’s a scratch-resistant coating and a nano-textured polymer layer that Apple says is up to 40% stiffer than competing materials. Underneath, high-strength glass sits above and below the OLED panel, using special adhesives that let the layers slide against one another as the display folds. Finally, a titanium plate underneath provides additional structural support.

Apple compares the way the layers move to the pages of a book, which helps explain how the display can repeatedly bend without putting excessive stress on any individual layer.

The second aspect is reducing the visibility of the crease that is there. To do that, Apple is returning to a familiar friend: nano-texture.

We’ve seen Apple’s nano-texture on several products in recent years, including the iPad Pro and MacBook Pro. Beyond serving as a matte finish and offering the usual benefits of nano-texture, it plays a central role in reducing crease visibility.

One way it minimizes crease visibility is by diffusing reflected light. In an interview, Tom Marieb, Apple’s VP of hardware, explained that the “specularity” of traditional glossy displays makes it “very easy to pick up topology differences.”

The nano-texture finish counteracts that on iPhone Duo by diffusing light and preventing the mirror-like reflections you get from a glossy display. Over the long term, the nano-texture finish will also be more forgiving of topology changes.

I’ve only used the iPhone Duo for a week, so I can’t speak to that long-term durability. In an interview with @angietutorials on TikTok, Kate Bergeron, Apple VP of Hardware Engineering, explained that the matte display coating is replaceable. 

I don’t think Apple expects iPhone Duo users to replace that cover layer because of crease visibility. Instead, it’s a repairability benefit. If the inner display is damaged, that cover layer can be replaced (for a surprisingly low price), without having to replace the entire display.

So, how does the iPhone Duo’s inner display fare in real-world use?

Using the inner display

Crease visibility

Put plainly, all that work Apple did to minimize crease visibility pays off.

Here’s the best way I can think of explaining it: anyone who says the iPhone Duo’s crease is invisible is misleading you. Even Apple doesn’t say that. It talks about the work it’s done to reduce the crease’s visibility, but nowhere does it claim the crease is invisible. At the same time, anyone who says the iPhone Duo’s crease is visible enough to be a problem is similarly misleading you.

The iPhone Duo’s crease isn’t visible when you use the device head-on in most lighting conditions. Yes, you can photograph the iPhone Duo at unflattering angles and clearly see the crease. People aren’t using the iPhone Duo at those angles, though.

The only time I could really see the crease during normal use was in brighter lighting, like sunlight, while looking at darker user interfaces, like a black loading screen or video frame. The combination of bright lights and darker software seems to be a perfect storm that accentuates the iPhone Duo’s crease.

The difference is between being able to see the crease when you’re looking for it and actually noticing it when you’re using the iPhone Duo. In my experience, the latter almost never happens.

You can feel the crease when using the iPhone Duo’s touchscreen, especially in portrait mode while scrolling webpages or social media. It is more noticeable than seeing the crease, but it’s still not a problem once you get used to it.

Beyond minimizing the crease, iPhone Duo’s nano-texture coating provides all the same benefits as nano-texture on other Apple products. It reduces glare and gives the screen a paper-like feel. It’s very similar to my 11-inch iPad Pro with a nano-texture display. The matte coating feels nice to the touch, though fingerprints are a bit harder to remove than on a normal glossy screen.

Another unique aspect of the iPhone Duo’s inner display is its under-screen FaceTime camera (more on that below). I’ve been impressed by how well the FaceTime camera blends in with the display. You can tell it’s there, but it’s not distracting when you’re looking straight on. There’s also a really nice animation where it shrinks down into itself after you finish using it.

Form factor

When you unfold the iPhone Duo, you’re presented with a 7.6-inch display. By screen area, Apple says the iPhone Duo’s display is 50% larger than the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s, 80% larger than the iPhone 18 Pro’s, and the largest display ever on an iPhone.

Unfolding the iPhone Duo and seeing that inner display is a remarkable experience. You’re taking a passport-sized device and unfolding it into what’s basically an iPad mini. Even after a week of using the iPhone Duo, that “wow factor” hasn’t worn off.

The iPhone Duo’s inner display has a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, giving it a wider, more rectangular shape than other foldables on the market. I’ve never found the taller, squarer shape of foldables like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra appealing. It’s essentially taping two normal-sized smartphones together for what I think is an unwieldy experience. The foldable aspect feels like an afterthought, whereas on the iPhone Duo it’s a key part of the experience.

If you’ve used an iPad, you’ll feel right at home when using the iPhone Duo’s inner display. It makes for a very natural experience when watching video with minimal letterboxing. The book-style design also bodes well for reading, browsing the web, and scrolling social media.

In my week with the iPhone Duo, I’ve found myself using the outer display when out and about, running errands. I’m using it basically like a normal iPhone. When I’m stationary, whether at home or at a coffee shop, I unfold it to use the larger screen.

I think this comes down to ergonomics. The iPhone Duo’s 7.6-inch inner display is simply too large to use comfortably one-handed, and it’s not particularly practical while walking around a grocery store. The outer display is much better suited for those situations.

I’m watching considerably more video on my iPhone Duo than I have on any previous iPhone. Compared to my iPhone 18 Pro, the added screen real estate makes it more enticing.

From a productivity standpoint, I can get more done with the iPhone Duo. Navigating WordPress is much easier than on an iPhone 18 Pro. I can see the full WordPress interface, rather than the awkward, long-and-tall mobile version that requires much more tapping between menus.

In the Mail app, I get a proper two-pane interface, so I can scroll my inbox on the left and read full emails on the right. It makes the triage process much easier. With Split View (more on that below), I can put Notes on one side and Safari on the other to prepare show notes for a podcast on iPhone Duo, rather than grabbing a Mac or an iPad.

The iPhone Duo gives you two very different experiences depending on what you’re doing. That’s what has surprised me most about it. I’m not going out of my way to find reasons to use the larger display. Those reasons have come naturally.

Software

It’s iOS 27

Amid all the rumors about iPhone Duo, there were many questions about its software and apps. Would it run iOS when folded and iPadOS when unfolded? Would it run a hybrid operating system? Would it run iOS but with iPad apps?

Ultimately, all of that was a waste of time. Instead, iPhone Duo runs the same iOS 27 foundation as every other iPhone, but with some key changes to accommodate the different screen sizes and aspect ratio. It’s not just normal iOS stretched (or shrunken) for the iPhone Duo’s screens.

The biggest change is that iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo moves many familiar navigation controls from the bottom to the right side of the interface. Using the Music app as an example, the navigation bar with things like “New” and “Library” now appears in a right-hand sidebar rather than at the bottom. Controls that normally appear at the top, such as the playlist button and three-dot menu in the Music app, have also shifted to the right-hand sidebar.

The changes go beyond just individual apps. On the Home Screen, the dock has been moved to the right-hand side. The status bar icons, like the time, Wi-Fi icon, and cellular bars (now dots), are in the upper-right corner above the dock.

The interface is adaptable, too. If you use the iPhone Duo unfolded and in portrait orientation, the dock and in-app navigation bars shift back to the bottom like “normal” iOS.

After a few days, Apple’s interface changes to accommodate the iPhone Duo’s form factor start to feel natural. They account for the shorter, wider aspect ratio; the smaller outer display; and the larger inner display.

Typing on the inner display while in portrait orientation is very natural. In landscape mode, you have to stretch a little bit, but it’s still doable for me.

The fluidity between all of it is fantastic. No matter how I held the iPhone Duo, UI elements were exactly where I expected them to be. There’s also that gorgeous software transition when you unfold or fold the iPhone Duo.

The iPhone Duo also supports Split View when unfolded—a first for any iPhone. You can place two apps side by side, or two windows from the same app. It’s the most powerful multitasking has ever been on an iPhone. Being able to put Safari on one side and Notes on the other has been a huge productivity boost for me on iPhone.

You can also pin a video to the top part of the screen, and use another app below it. That app will morph to fill the size of the display below it.

Apps

Speaking of apps, we need to talk about the different ways apps behave on the iPhone Duo. First, all of Apple’s pre-installed apps have been updated to take full advantage of the iPhone Duo’s two displays. This includes proper right-aligned controls that float alongside the content as you scroll in apps like News, Maps, Music, and Reminders.

The second part of the app story is third-party apps, which gets a bit more complicated. Every existing iPhone app works on iPhone Duo. This means that any iPhone app you have today will run on iPhone Duo. From here, there are basically three tiers.

First, apps built with the iOS 26 SDK or earlier don’t take full advantage of iPhone Duo. The example above shows the MLB app running on iPhone Duo. In landscape mode, it has large black bars on either side of the app. In portrait orientation, it runs floating in the center, surrounded by letterboxing on all sides.

You can then zoom in like you can when running an iPhone app on iPad. If the app supports landscape mode, you can also manually switch between portrait and landscape interfaces, as shown in the Google Docs screenshots above.

Second, there are apps built with the iOS 27 SDK. These apps resize to fill most of the inner display, but leave space along the right edge for the status bar. The above screenshots show the Reddit app running on the iPhone Duo:

Here’s what YouTube looks like: 

And here is what X looks like: 

Finally, there are apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later. These apps can be fully optimized for iPhone Duo, using the entire inner and outer displays. In just the week I’ve had the iPhone Duo, developers big and small have rolled out a ton of apps fully optimized for iPhone Duo.

There is a huge difference between using an app updated for iPhone Duo and one that isn’t. Going forward, I think proper iPhone Duo support will be a deciding factor when I choose which apps to use. If I’m choosing between two apps that do the same thing and only one is optimized for the iPhone Duo, I’ll choose that one.

I’ve tried a ton of third-party apps with iPhone Duo support over the last week, and below are some of my favorites.

More iPad, please

I wish there were more iPadOS elements sprinkled throughout the iPhone Duo’s software. It’s great having Split View, but I wish there was an iPadOS-like way to drag and drop apps into that Split View interface. Slide Over also seems like a piece of low-hanging fruit.

There are places where iOS isn’t doing enough to take full advantage of that 7.6-inch inner display. For comparison, the iPad mini has an 8.3-inch display, and it runs the full iPadOS interface. Even the previous generation 7.9-inch iPad mini got the full iPadOS experience at the time.

One of my favorite things about using an iPad is that websites (mostly) treat Safari as a desktop-class browser. That’s not the case on iPhone Duo, where you sometimes get the awkward mobile layout even when browsing on the unfolded inner display. This doesn’t always happen (hence my WordPress example earlier), but I wish it were closer to the desktop-class iPad experience.

To be clear, I don’t think the iPhone Duo should run iPadOS. I think going all-in on iOS was the right decision. I just want iOS to do more in certain areas to really show off the benefits of the bigger screen. Right now, I sometimes have to fight to get iOS to recognize I’m using an iPhone with a 7.6-inch display. 

Touch ID vs Face ID

Perhaps the biggest trade-off with the iPhone Duo is that it uses Touch ID instead of Face ID. Flagship iPhones have used Face ID since the iPhone X in 2017, so this is a big change.

iPhone Duo has Touch ID integrated into the side button. I’ve added both my thumbs and index fingers, so it’s easy to unlock the iPhone Duo no matter how I’m holding it. It also supports “Rest to Open,” so you can authenticate with Touch ID and keep your finger on the side button to unlock it automatically.

I think switching from Face ID to Touch ID has been the hardest thing to get used to on iPhone Duo. I’ve become so accustomed to just looking at my iPhone to unlock it. Having to deliberately reach for the side button feels like a step backward, even though Touch ID works quickly and reliably.

One benefit I have enjoyed: Touch ID is a lot easier to use when your iPhone is lying flat on a table. Instead of picking up your iPhone to unlock it with Face ID, you can rest your finger on the Touch ID sensor and to glance at your locked notifications.

iPhone Duo also supports Apple Watch unlock. If you enable this feature, you can swipe up on your iPhone Duo’s lock screen, and it will automatically unlock if you’re wearing your Apple Watch (so long as your Apple Watch has a passcode on it and is unlocked).

I used my iPhone Duo without Apple Watch unlock enabled for the first few days to get a feel for what it’s like to use an iPhone with Touch ID for the first time in nearly a decade. Ultimately, I turned on Apple Watch unlock, and it does make the experience significantly better.

Finally, because iPhone Duo doesn’t have Face ID, it also doesn’t have any Attention Aware features. On Face ID-enabled iPhones, your iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts. Of all those features, I really miss being able to glance at my iPhone and have my notifications automatically expand.

Ultimately, Touch ID works just fine on the iPhone Duo. It takes a while to get used to, but Apple Watch unlock helps quite a bit. I assume Face ID is on the shortlist of features for future iPhone Duo generations.

Cameras

Despite being Apple’s most expensive iPhone, the iPhone Duo does not have its most powerful camera system. On paper, many of the Main camera specs are similar to the iPhone Air and iPhone 17, but Apple emphasizes that it designed the camera specifically for the iPhone Duo’s ultra-thin form factor.

The iPhone Duo also features a 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide camera, which is the same camera found in the iPhone 18 Pro. Its specifications also match the Ultra Wide camera on the regular iPhone 17.

I’ve found the Main camera on iPhone Duo to perform just as well as the camera on the iPhone Air I’ve been using as my primary iPhone for the past year. It’s a notch below the iPhone 18 Pro, but it’s not a dramatic difference. 

Here are some comparison shots between the iPhone Duo (left) and iPhone 18 Pro (right): 

iPhone Duo (left) and iPhone 18 Pro (right)

iPhone Duo (left) and iPhone 18 Pro (right)

iPhone Duo (left) and iPhone 18 Pro (right)

iPhone Duo (left) and iPhone 18 Pro (right)

The iPhone Duo also features a 12MP Center Stage camera on its outer display. That’s a step down from the 18MP Center Stage camera found on the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and iPhone 18 Pro. You still get features like automatic framing and Dual Capture, but the Duo uses a lower-resolution camera with a smaller ƒ/2.2 aperture.

But that’s not all. The iPhone Duo actually has one more camera: a FaceTime camera located underneath the inner display.

The FaceTime camera itself is nothing to write home about, but it does get the job done for FaceTime calls. It’s a measly 4MP sensor, but it supports Center Stage and 1080p video recording. If I’m on a video call or just taking a quick selfie, the under-display FaceTime camera is perfectly adequate. For anything more demanding, I’d choose a different camera.

But that’s one of the most unique things about the iPhone Duo’s form factor. You can use the 48MP rear cameras to take selfies. By unfolding the device and flipping it around, you can use the outer display as a live viewfinder while taking pictures with the higher-quality Main or Ultra Wide cameras. This means you can frame your shot and see exactly what the cameras see, without relying on the dedicated front-facing camera.

The same concept also works when someone else is taking your picture. With a feature Apple calls Duo Preview, the outer display shows a live preview of the shot, letting you check your framing and adjust your pose while the person behind the camera takes the photo.

The iPhone Duo also features Smart Take, which uses on-device AI to automatically capture a photo when everyone is posed and ready. You can prop the iPhone Duo up on a surface, activate Smart Take, and step into the frame without having to race against a timer.

Ultimately, the iPhone Duo isn’t the best camera Apple sells today. It’s a very good camera, but it’s not on the same level as the iPhone 18 Pro. That said, the versatile form factor of the iPhone Duo opens it up to new ways to use the camera hardware. As someone who used the iPhone Air up until the iPhone 18 Pro’s launch last month, I’m pretty used to life without a telephoto camera. I’d absolutely prefer having one, but it’s a tradeoff I’m willing to accept for the other benefits of the iPhone Duo’s form factor.

Odds and ends

Battery life

Here’s what Apple says about the iPhone Duo’s battery life:

Video playback on the outer display: Up to 44 hours

Video playback on the inner display: Up to 31 hours

Typical mixed use: Up to 24 hours

That “typical use” number is based on a “combination of passive and active use of a variety of applications, including but not limited to messaging, photos, music, social media, video streaming, games, web browsing, and navigation.” For iPhone Duo, the number also assumes you use both screens equally.

The iPhone Duo features a unique dual-battery architecture, with one battery in each half of the device to maximize capacity. Apple uses custom silicon and software algorithms to manage charging, discharging, and balancing between the two batteries. This lets them operate as essentially a single battery.

In my testing, the iPhone Duo has more than enough battery life to last me through a normal day. I can take it off the charger, use it normally throughout the day, and have around 20% remaining by the end of the day. I haven’t done any formal battery testing, but I’d estimate that around 60% of my usage has been on the inner display, with the remaining 40% on the outer display.

Speakers

Apple says it optimized the iPhone Duo’s speaker placement and audio tuning to deliver Spatial Audio no matter how you hold the device. That includes using it fully open, closed, or partially folded in seated and tent configurations.

I do think the iPhone Duo’s speakers leave a little bit to be desired. I wasn’t overly impressed with the speaker quality, and I think there’s a notable disparity compared with the iPhone 18 Pro. The iPhone Duo’s speakers sound thinner and quieter to my ears.

MagSafe

The iPhone Duo features MagSafe support, despite early rumors to the contrary. Existing MagSafe stands and chargers should work with the iPhone Duo. I’ve tested it with charging stands from Twelve South and Belkin so far, and haven’t had any problems.

MagSafe accessories like wallets and batteries, however, are a different story. Because the iPhone Duo is shorter than a normal iPhone, these accessories will likely hang off the bottom. This includes my beloved MagSafe Wallet straight from Apple. I suspect third-party options will pop up soon, but right now the options are pretty limited.

Performance

The iPhone Duo is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, the same chip found in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. In my testing, performance has been essentially identical to the iPhone 18 Pro. Everything feels fast and fluid, including using Split View on the inner display.

Apple has also developed a custom thermal architecture for the iPhone Duo, including a vapor chamber and flexible graphite to help dissipate heat across its two halves. I do think the iPhone Duo runs a bit hotter than the iPhone 18 Pro, but not in a way that impacts performance.

For a deeper dive into A20 Pro performance, I have a bunch of charts in my iPhone 18 Pro review.

No Action button

The iPhone Duo doesn’t have an Action button, but it does have a Camera Control. I’d gladly swap them if given the option, and I imagine most people would agree. I’ve become accustomed to using the Action button to quickly open my AI app of choice, so its absence on the iPhone Duo is disappointing.

9to5Mac Take

Foldable smartphones have been around for years in various shapes and sizes. When most people think of foldables, I think they picture form factors like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which looks a lot more like a “normal” smartphone that happens to unfold.

The iPhone Duo doesn’t look anything like a “normal” smartphone. It’s awkward and weird on the surface, and that will turn some people off. But as soon as you unfold the iPhone Duo, it expands into an iPad-like device that is instantly recognizable.

After a week with the iPhone Duo, I’m convinced that this form factor represents the future of the iPhone. There’s something special about a compact, notebook-like iPhone that unfolds into a tablet-like experience, and it just makes sense once you start using it. Importantly, neither screen feels compromised. I’ve been repeatedly surprised by how capable the outer display is compared to what I expected. 

That said, the iPhone Duo is a first-generation product, and it comes with trade-offs. From a hardware perspective, most people will notice two things: it has Touch ID rather than Face ID, and it lacks a telephoto camera.

I also think there are aspects of the software experience that need to catch up to the hardware. Apple’s overarching software philosophy is on the right track, but there are places where iOS could do more to take advantage of the larger inner display.

At $1,999, the iPhone Duo is an expensive proposition, especially when you consider the features you’re giving up compared to the iPhone 18 Pro. For most people, a traditional iPhone is still the practical purchase right now. 

But over time, I think that calculation will change. The iPhone Duo is a glimpse at the future of the iPhone, and that future is foldable.

title: Some Google Home Speakers downloading massive amounts of data in the background
snippet: The new Google Home Speaker has an issue where it downloads hundreds of gigabytes of data in the background for some owners. more…
fullText:
The new Google Home Speaker has an issue where it downloads hundreds of gigabytes of data in the background for some owners.

Over the past week, several reports have emerged about how the Google Home Speaker appears to be continuously downloading data from company servers.

In my case, a Google Home Speaker that has not been used in the past day for voice commands or media streaming consumed 17 GB of data in 24 hours. At 3 a.m. PT, it downloaded 9.99 GB. Given the timing, this could be related to failed attempts to download device firmware. 

Meanwhile, on October 13, the same speaker downloaded 41 GB of data. Over the past 30 days, the total download comes in at 132 GB.

	

It’s not clear if this is a widespread issue. Another lightly used Home Speaker of ours (in a different household) downloaded only 2 GB of data in the past month. 

	

Most routers let you check how much data a particular device has used. If you’re using Nest Wifi, go to the Google Home app’s Wifi top tab > Devices > select your speaker > Device usage graphs. You can switch between 1-, 7-, and 30-day graphs.

We’re not seeing this download issue with other Google Home and Nest devices, including several Nest Hubs in the same house as the affected Home Speaker.

If you have multiple Home Speakers and a limited data plan, this issue could easily breach your cap, as some have found.

In a statement to 9to5Google today, the company acknowledged the issue and said “a fix is already rolling out that should address this for users.”

title: Apple is looking for a cellular modem engineer to help shape its transition to 6G
snippet: Apple is looking for an experienced cellular modem systems engineer to help develop its next generation of cellular modems as the company transitions toward 6G. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is looking for an experienced cellular modem systems engineer to help develop its next generation of cellular modems as the company transitions toward 6G. Here are the details.

‘A rare opportunity to shape the future of wireless communication’

As spotted by MacRumors, Apple listed a new job opening yesterday for a 6G Cellular Modem Systems Engineer, with a base salary range of $175,000 to $308,500 per year, plus stock awards and other benefits.

From the job listing:

We’re looking for a Cellular Modem Systems Engineer to join our cellular systems engineering team as we define and build the next generation of cellular technology. This is a rare opportunity to shape the future of wireless communication at a company that ships at global scale as we transition towards 6G. In this role, you’ll bring an end-to-end view of wireless systems — spanning 3GPP standards, feature definition and planning, design, hardware and software architecture and partitioning — to deliver leading-edge performance and power optimizations and features that directly improve the user experience across Apple products. If you thrive at the intersection of deep technical theory and hands-on bring-up — and you’re excited about pushing beyond 5G into the 6G era — we want to hear from you.

Apple says the candidate’s responsibilities will include defining features and requirements for next-generation cellular modems, designing algorithms to improve performance and power efficiency, and working with hardware and software teams to bring those technologies to market.

The candidate should have a degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering, or a related field, along with at least 10 years of industry experience working with cellular technologies.

Apple also requires a strong understanding of cellular communication standards and proficiency in MATLAB, C/C++, or Python.

Interestingly, Apple also lists experience with generative AI and LLM-based tools “to accelerate engineering workflows” as a minimum qualification. Ideally, the candidate should also have a track record of published research or patents in wireless communications, among other preferred qualifications.

For context, 6G is still years away and in the early stages of development, as companies and industry organizations work to define what it will look like.

	

The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has outlined potential peak speeds of up to 200 Gbps, compared to 5G’s theoretical maximum of 20 Gbps, along with research targets for latency as low as 0.1 milliseconds.

AI is also expected to play a much bigger role in 6G, helping networks automatically adjust to changing conditions, optimize signal quality, manage traffic, and reduce power consumption.

The first official 6G technical specifications are expected to be finalized in late 2028, with commercial networks and compatible devices anticipated around 2030.

title: Final Payday: Aces High playtest on Meta Quest and Steam comes with a free mask this week
snippet: Payday’s first full-VR game is on the cusp of release, but you don’t have to wait! Join the playtest now and get exclusive rewards when the full game releases on November 5. more…
fullText:
Payday’s first full-VR game is on the cusp of release, but you don’t have to wait! Join the playtest now and get exclusive rewards when the full game releases on November 5.

It’s almost hard to believe we’re getting such a big-name VR release like Payday: Aces High this late in 2026, but the release is almost upon us, and the second public play test has already begun! The free playtest runs from October 19 through 26 on Steam and Meta Quest, and you can take part in the final Payday: Aces High playtest by visiting the store page on Steam and this Meta Quest link.

Players who join this week will earn a limited edition Kitty mask, which is exclusive to the play test. Nothing like looking elite just because you played a free game, right? The final game debuts on November 5 on Meta Quest, SteamVR, and Steam Frame for $24.99 USD.

Not familiar with the Payday series? Maybe you’ve been hiding in a bank vault for the past decade and a half, but the concept is pretty simple. You and three other “professionals” take on missions to rob higher and higher profile targets, grabbing as much sweet loot along the way as you can.

	

Meta Quest 3S on Amazon

Payday: Aces High rewards players for stealth and clever play, meaning you earn more on missions you don’t botch. The co-op gameplay requires real teamwork if you want to last, and the VR version takes this to new heights with natural body language and emotions, plus an entirely new story with new protagonists (called The Aces) to play as. As players earn cash and other in-game currency, they can unlock new weapons, traps, masks, and abilities, so your time is fully rewarded.

I got to play an early version of Payday: Aces High back in August, plus the first play test, and as a fan of the series, I can tell you this is an incredible entry. This week’s play test includes a second mission that wasn’t in the first play test, so you can rack up even more experience before going into the final game in a few weeks. The final game will have around seven missions at launch, with additional ones planned for after release.

What are you waiting for? Slap on that VR headset, plan those heists, and feel great about the big payoff.

title: Android Auto ‘Work Account’ support would allow for easy switching in work vehicles
snippet: Support for work accounts was recently discovered in an unreleased version of Android Auto. It could be a perfect feature for users who need to connect to their work vehicle without personal apps enabled. more…
fullText:
Support for work accounts was recently discovered in an unreleased version of Android Auto. It could be a perfect feature for users who need to connect to their work vehicle without personal apps enabled.

Android has an existing separation of data for work apps. Work Accounts lets users divide personal and business accounts, isolating the data and applications between them. For users who have Work Profiles enabled, a small briefcase icon signifies whether these apps are turned on or accessible. Those apps then run in separate instances.

Android Auto has not and still does not officially support Work Profiles. But an unreleased version of the app shows signs of support, discovered by Android Authority. The Android Auto build (18.0.664204) adds Work Account to the Quick Settings tile options.

Similar to how it functions on mobile Android, enabling it lights up a briefcase icon over the app drawer, so you know those app versions are enabled. The test version isn’t fully functional, but it may mean Google is planning to add a critical function for some users to Android Auto.

	

Work Account support in Android Auto would be a great addition for work or corporate vehicles. Those who spend work hours behind the wheel are missing out on support for those apps, hindering the experience Android Auto tries to provide.

There’s no telling if or when Work Accounts get support in Android Auto, but it’s appearance signals it might be soon.

title: Samsung’s Android 18-based One UI 10 update sounds like it might be a big deal
snippet: While Android 17 is still trickling out to Android phones, Samsung is undoubtedly cooking up its Android 18-based One UI 10 update behind the scenes and, based on some early leaks, it at least sounds like it could be a reasonably big one. more…
fullText:
While Android 17 is still trickling out to Android phones, Samsung is undoubtedly cooking up its Android 18-based One UI 10 update behind the scenes and, based on some early leaks, it at least sounds like it could be a reasonably big one.

One UI 10 rumors call the update ‘significant’ 

Rumors about Samsung tend to get overhyped. Tiny details get too much attention and there’s always some drama mixed in for good measure.

That said, early rumblings around One UI 10 make it sound like there’s actually something worth being excited about. Ice Universe says that the update will bring “significant changes, unprecedented in nature.” Also having popped up is the term “Galaxy OS,” though there’s not been much weight behind that both in terms of where it came from and that the rumor itself doubles back on that name. 

In both cases, though, a big update is claimed to be in the works.

	

Samsung is overdue for an overhaul, but what will it be?

While there’s not much to talk about in terms of actual features yet, Samsung is due for a bigger update this year.

The last major update to One UI came with One UI 7 back in 2024, bringing with it overhauls to the lockscreen, app drawer, and more. The roots of that update arrived in One UI 6 a year prior, but it was the Android 15 update that brought the welcome overhaul.

Since then, Samsung’s updates have been pretty tame. One UI 8 (Android 16) delivered quality-of-life tweaks and some app updates while One UI 8.5 later built on that with some Liqud Glass clones and more design and functionality tweaks.

One UI 9, based on Android 17, is currently rolling out and it’s one of the smallest updates in recent memory. 

One UI 9: All the features you need to know [Video]

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

What could One UI 10 bring to the table? It’s genuinely hard to know at this point. Virtually every other Android brand has been diving into straight-up Liquid Glass clones lately, and there’s no reason to think Samsung won’t succumb to the same. 

Making it harder to know what’s on the way is that we don’t know much about Android 18 itself yet. Google has teased some new graphics features that developers can leverage and it doesn’t feel like much of a leap to assume that Samsung could lean into that. Google teased “delightful mesh gradients” and “progressive blurs” powered by these new features, with the Android Dev Summit set to detail more on that next week. 

What would you want from One UI 10? Let us know in the comments below!

title: Wyze’s latest weight scale has a display you can actually see, Google Health sync
snippet: Wyze has released a new BodyScan Plus scale that syncs with Google Health and Android Health Connect while fixing a long-running problem with scales – this one actually lets you see the display. more…
fullText:
Wyze has released a new BodyScan Plus scale that syncs with Google Health and Android Health Connect while fixing a long-running problem with scales – this one actually lets you see the display.

Available starting today as a part of “Wyze Week,” the Wyze Scale Ultra BodyScan Plus continues its mouthful of a name, but with some nice features to back it up.

The Wyze Scale Ultra Bodyscan launched in late 2025 with this new Plus model being its sequel. It’s a bit more expensive at $149 – what isn’t more expensive in 2026 – and makes one key hardware change. Where the original made itself stand out by putting sensors on a bar that you could raise up to get more details on muscle mass and more, it still put the display at your feet, making it a bit harder to see those results. 

Wyze Scale Ultra Bodyscan Plus moves the display over to that bar, letting you see everything way closer to eye level. 

	

When just tracking weight without the added sensors, the display is still at your feet, but the bar lets you lift that up for easier readability. 

That’s on top of the scale supporting the same metrics including “weight, BMI, body fat percentage, muscle mass, body water, visceral fat, protein, bone mass, basal metabolic rate,” and others. The scale requires no subscription, nor does it even require a Bluetooth connection to your phone. Built-in Wi-Fi means it can sync with the Wyze app on its own while also being able to connect into Google Health and Apple Health, as well as leverage Android’s Health Connect to tie into other apps. 

Wyze Scale Ultra Bodyscan Plus is available today for $149.

title: Photographer Tyler Stalman reviews iPhone Duo’s new cameras
snippet: iPhone Duo is almost here, and our in-depth 9to5Mac review was published today. While that review offers plenty of insights into iPhone Duo’s cameras, if you want a professional photographer’s take, Tyler Stalman’s new video has you covered. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is almost here, and our in-depth 9to5Mac review was published today. While that review offers plenty of insights into iPhone Duo’s cameras, if you want a professional photographer’s take, Tyler Stalman’s new video has you covered.

Here’s how iPhone Duo’s camera system compares to iPhone 18 Pro, per Tyler Stalman

One main drawback of the iPhone Duo compared to iPhone 18 Pro is its camera system.

Not only does the Duo lack a Telephoto lens, but its Main camera isn’t quite as good, and the Center Stage front camera is a step down too.

But many prospective iPhone Duo buyers might be wondering: exactly how noticeable are the differences between Duo and iPhone 18 Pro cameras?

Photographer Tyler Stalman published his video review today. Here’s what he says about the Main camera:

Most people are not going to spot the difference. They look very similar in most lighting conditions…Even in low light, the Pro is better, but I think it’s probably not going to jump out to most people.

Of course, it’s hard to judge whether “most people” will include you. For example, 9to5Mac’s review said the Duo’s camera is comparable to iPhone Air’s—which specs confirm. And personally, I’ve found iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera a big improvement over the Air camera.

Moving beyond picture quality though, Stalman highlights how the camera experience with iPhone Duo has an edge. He explains how great it is that iPhone Duo’s two screens let you take 48MP selfies, and when you’re photographing others, they can see what you’re seeing.

Regarding the Ultra Wide lens, Stalman says that iPhone Duo seems to offer basically the same quality as iPhone 18 Pro.

The Center Stage Front Camera, however, is another area where iPhone Duo lags iPhone 18 Pro. It’s a 12MP camera, while iPhone 18 Pro and even last year’s 17 Pro use an 18MP lens.

Stalman says to expect selfie quality similar to pre-iPhone 17 models, but with the benefit of features like Center Stage and automatic framing so you can hold your iPhone in any orientation.

Again though, the iPhone Duo’s selfie camera isn’t as important as on iPhone 18 Pro, since you have the option of taking selfies with the Main camera. But it’s worth noting the differences anyways.

title: Google TV powers the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro glasses, and that’s exactly the problem
snippet: The Google TV platform is amazing on the big screen, but its limitations make it more frustrating than it should be on the mobile RayNeo Pocket TV Pro. more…
fullText:
The Google TV platform is amazing on the big screen, but its limitations make it more frustrating than it should be on the mobile RayNeo Pocket TV Pro.

Google TV is the best thing that’s possibly ever happened to my TV. I switched to the Google TV Streamer about a year ago after my Roku streamer broke down, and I haven’t looked back. So when I got the chance to try the Google TV-powered RayNeo Pocket TV Pro — a TV remote-like device that hooks up to RayNeo smart glasses and even has 12-bit Dolby Vision support — I was ecstatic. This would be a dream come true on my next flight!

The setup was dead easy, and I was on the Play Store downloading all my favorite streaming apps within a minute. I loaded Netflix, found a few shows to keep me occupied for a few hours in an uncomfortable coach airplane seat, and went to hit that shiny red download button. Alas, the download button didn’t exist.

Surely this was a mistake? Maybe that show just didn’t support offline downloads. I found another one and ran into the same problem. Turns out, the Netflix app on the Google TV platform doesn’t support offline downloads. Major bummer, but that’s alright; I’ve got like half a dozen other streaming apps to choose from.

	

Unfortunately, every single streaming app doesn’t support offline downloads on the Google TV platform. Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, HBO, even YouTube all don’t support offline downloads on the entire Google TV platform. I was befuddled. How could this have possibly slipped past testing, let alone into a final product? The RayNeo Pocket TV Pro went back into the box, and there it sat for over a week until I returned from my trip.

The personal pocket TV for your home

Essentially, I was in the “you’re holding it wrong” kind of scenario with this product, but I imagine I won’t be the last person who thought you could use it like this. For me, this is now a useless product, because there’s never a time when I want to sit and watch something without my family. For someone else, however, this might be the actual dream product I originally thought it was, just for a very different individual.

Let’s say you love watching live sports, but your family outvoted you and is now on the main TV. A quick tap of the “Live TV” button on the remote will take you to the Google FreePlay app, where you can find a metric ton of free live content, including plenty of games to catch. You could also load up Hulu, ESPN, Amazon, or whatever other service might be airing the actual game you want to watch, too, since this is a full Google TV device.

Or, hey, maybe you want to catch up on the latest Knives Out movie, but you’ve got little kids who probably would have nightmares if they watched a murder mystery before bed. Slap on a pair of RayNeo GT smart glasses, plug it into the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro, and you’re watching Knives Out in a perfectly private cinema while your kids watch Moana for the 400th time.

RayNeo Pocket TV Pro at Amazon

RayNeo GT smart glasses at Amazon

All this is aided by a piece of hardware that feels absolutely perfect. The remote looks virtually identical to any Google TV streamer you can buy and weighs 208g, which is the same weight as the average smartphone. The large, circular directional pad makes navigation a breeze, and the prominent microphone button calls up Gemini instantly, so you can find anything in a few seconds.

Even the battery life is quite good, lasting around 5 hours or so on a single charge. It’s got a dedicated USB-C port on the bottom for smart glasses output, and a separate port for charging, so you could plug this into an outlet or any portable battery (like this Anker Prime one) and keep it going for even longer. There’s even a microSD card port on the side for people who own digital copies of movies or TV shows, which would have fixed my problem if I did.

And as a full-fledged Google TV device, this one has every single app you know and love from your actual TV in your house. There’s quite literally no difference in the software; it’s just ultra-private now that it works on a pair of smart glasses. The only way it would get better is, of course, if the same streaming apps that allow offline downloads on phones worked here.

title: Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world
snippet: OnePlus is dead. The enthusiast-focused brand turned Oppo for the rest of the world was shuttered, ironically only for the rest of the world, earlier this year and its memory loomed large over my past few weeks using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. For as great is this phone is, it’s a sad reminder that phones like these are going to be lacking in some parts of the world going forward, and that’s a crying shame. more…
fullText:
OnePlus is dead. The enthusiast-focused brand turned Oppo for the rest of the world was shuttered, ironically only for the rest of the world, earlier this year and its memory loomed large over my past few weeks using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. For as great is this phone is, it’s a sad reminder that phones like these are going to be lacking in some parts of the world going forward, and that’s a crying shame.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a beast on paper, though not quite the Find X9 Ultra I fell head over heels for earlier this year. To quickly summarize what you’re getting here (specifically for the EU variant):

6.78-inch AMOLED display (144Hz, LTPO, 3,600 nits peak brightness, 3,840Hz PWM)

MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro

12GB RAM

512GB UFS 4.1

7,150 mAh battery

80W wired/50W wireless charging (no Qi2 magnets)

Ultrasonic fingerprint sensor + camera-based face unlock

Cameras: 200MP main, 200MP 13mm ultrawide, 200MP 70mm (3x optical) telephoto, 50MP front-facing

By basically every measurement, a true flagship. The cameras, as mentioned, aren’t quite at the level of the Find X9 Ultra, but it’s still impressive to see three 200MP sensors on board here.

And those cameras perform very well.

	

Oppo touts killer video from this setup, including 4K/60fps, 4K/120fps, and 8K/30fps from every rear-facing lens, as well as improvements to HDR and stabilization. These can certainly go a long way in creator spaces, and I was impressed at the quality even in more casual use cases. Oppo worked with Instagram, for example, to improve uploads from the Find X10 series and the results speak for themselves.

As per usual, I found myself mostly using the camera here for stills, and I still find myself loving the experience of shooting on an Oppo flagship. Shots are generally crisp and clean, and the app is very easy to use despite all of the options it builds in. Compared to the Ultra I last used, I found myself wishing the telephoto lens had more range, as the 3x optical zoom quickly felt its limits kicking in. Oppo supports up to 120x hybrid zoom, but the quality falls off long before that, and the AI-powered enhancements really struggle to bridge the gap on anything beyond 10x. I wish the company had just used a 5x lens here rather than 3x. Still, most shots I took were excellent, and that 3x lens is the best shooter of the bunch, producing excellent natural bokeh in its shots. The 200MP sensor and Oppo’s software go a long way in ensuring that anything in the 3x-8x range, give or take, comes out at full quality. Not to mention the color processing – it nailed the colors of an absolutely gorgeous sunset I captured a couple of weeks ago. My Pixel would never. 

Adding on Oppo’s 10x teleconverter takes the whole thing up a notch, with levels of natural bokeh that just aren’t achievable on a smartphone otherwise. It’s not as crisp as a “real” camera with the same lens setup, but the results are often stunning.

View full-size samples on Google Photos.

But, outside of the camera, how does the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max hold up?

Frankly, very well. 

The hardware itself is fantastic. I reviewed the “Lumos White” trim which is a tiny bit lighter than others, but it’s still a fairly hefty phone regardless. I don’t mind the weight, though, when a phone is delivering powerful camera hardware. The same goes for the camera bump which pops out of the back quite a ways. I do loathe that Oppo opted for this dual-size camera bump where the main square off to the left is taller than the secondary bump used to house the flash and color-focused camera lens. It results in a phone that rocks back and forth on a table when not in a case, despite such an obvious solution sitting right there. It’s annoying, but I do appreciate other touches here such as the knurling around the camera lens and the splash of orange from the Hasselblad partnership (though the little ridge picks up dust like crazy).

This is where I’ll throw in the mention that I found myself using Oppo’s carbon fiber case throughout my entire review period, not because I felt the phone needed a case, but because this is yet another Android flagship forgoing built-in Qi2 magnets. The excuses are just lame at this point, especially with Oppo pretty heavily investing in magnetic accessories. It’s getting old saying this in every review, but I’m going to keep bringing it up until it becomes the standard it should be.

The frame has power and volume buttons off to the right side and they’re as tactile and satisfying as ever, while a “Snap Key” on the opposite side is a blatant clone of Apple’s Action Button, right down to the UI used to customize it. Still, I appreciate the shortcut and use it for the flashlight/torch, but I wish Oppo would take this up a notch with single-press and double-press actions, rather than limiting it solely to the long-press that Apple uses. While we’re on that topic, I wish Oppo would finally adopt the double-press power button gesture for activating the camera in global markets. This phone has a great camera, but lacking this shortcut is an absolute pain.

The display is gorgeous, as you’d expect from any modern flagship, and the built-in screen protector has held up remarkably well over roughly a month of use. 

As for the software, ColorOS 17 very much leans into the whole Liquid Glass clone trend, and I’m not a fan. But, to Oppo’s credit, you can easily tone down the transparency to get a much more visually pleasing design. That won’t change the Apple copycat looks found throughout system apps, but it makes it a much better experience on the whole.

I’ve always been more of a fan of Pixel UI and even One UI over most Chinese Android skins, but ColorOS has grown on me. Once you get over the initial learning curve, it’s a very user-friendly experience in so many ineffable ways. It’s truly hard to describe why it’s a pleasure to use, but I find myself with fewer complaints. They’re still there, of course – just a couple of quick hitters: Notification icons disappear inconsistently, the lockscreen shows notifications on top of the fingerprint icon which leads to a lot of misclicks, etc – but I find myself overall still feeling comfortable using ColorOS nowadays.

And it runs smooth just as promised. That’s probably in part thanks to Oppo’s continued optimizations, but also the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro under the hood. The chip also stays cool. I threw everything from high-GPS use, 90°F days to video exports and more at this phone, and it never once warmed up even a little bit. Are we missing out without these MediaTek flagships in the States? Maybe!

Finally, let’s talk battery life.

The silicon-carbon battery here gives the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max a whopping 7,150 mAh battery in the EU, and the endurance rocks. This is not quite a 2-day phone in my testing thus far, but even heavy days won’t kill it. Whether I was running hotspots, editing videos, or playing games, Find X10 Pro Max never ended a day below 30%. I would imagine the 8,000 mAh version found in other regional variants pushes it over the edge of being a 2-day phone, but the point is you’ll be happy with this battery life. And, thanks to speedy SuperVOOC and USB-C PD charging on board, I never found myself needing to plug this phone in overnight. It almost acts like a smartwatch – a quick charge while I’m in the shower and getting ready for the day has been plenty to keep it topped off most of the time.

And after using all of that for a few weeks, I’m just about as sad about the situation surrounding this phone as I have been happy in using it.

The end of OnePlus means that Oppo phones like this one simply aren’t coming Stateside anymore. Of course, OnePlus’ versions were typically diluted compared to Oppo’s anyway (and that’s even true with the OnePlus 16), but it was better than nothing. It’s increasingly frustrating to be losing out on devices like these in the States, because Android brands like Oppo have been massively stepping up on quality in recent years.

Pricing, though, is against this one. In Europe, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is €1,799. That’s a crazy amount of money for a smartphone that doesn’t fold.

If you live in a region where the Find X10 series is for sale, I think you’ll be thrilled by the Pro Max. The standard Find X10 Pro is not one to sleep on either. It’s a bit smaller despite having the same battery, and the cameras aren’t too far behind. 

					

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a complete package, with excellent cameras and battery life, and speedy software.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Triple 200MP cameras

											

Excellent battery life

											

ColorOS is quietly one of the best Android skins

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Smaller battery on EU models

											

No Qi2 magnets

											

Very high pricing
